text:
There have been three key critiques in regards to the @prlnet  raise, but they are largely overblown in my view:

(1) The lab sells AI for dollars and keeps any PEARL it mines, so its investors can profit even if pearl-2:native falls. 

But PEARL is meant to be a SoV like Bitcoin, so buybacks would start a classic fight over how much of the lab’s revenue goes to shareholders vs token holders. The lab raised its own money to build a business that earns separately. That is the separation the SoV narrative actually needs, and the raise allows the lab to not sell the PEARL it may have for funding.

(2) The lab has written every fork and therefore controls the network and would cater to itself. 

But a fork only sticks if the majority of hashrate runs it and the lab’s $75M fleet would add only 2% to 3%. More importantly, the network won’t survive unless someone actually proves useful mining works, so the lab pushing to prove it outweighs the risk of its control.

(3) The lab has never disclosed how much PEARL it holds and the whitepaper says the low starting difficulty was partly meant to fund the team behind it. 

But the raise was cash for shares and not a token sale, and while we can’t tell which addresses are the lab’s, 98% of the coins mined in launch week have never moved. Although more transparency around their current holdings would help the market give more confidence around the entity.

If you agree or disagree let me know...

text:
我最近一直在研究“抗量子公链”这个赛道，这个概念并不新鲜，从我前几篇的推文介绍中可以看到2018年就已经有相关的公链了，所以为什么？

这个 “为什么” 实际上是两个问题：
1. 为什么选择研究这个赛道？
2. 为什么是现在？

先回答第1️⃣个问题：

（1）随着量子技术的发展，它会被越来越多的提及，它会有持续不断的叙事热度；

（2）虽然现在“量子计算机”并没有问世，但是这是一个很难被证伪的赛道，特别是在中美都在大力发展这项技术的前提下，即使不幸最后被证伪，也是一个长期的过程，这个叙事具有长期持续性；

（3）我判断：未来抗量子会成为标配。所以这里面就会蕴含着很多的机会，老公链升级的机会，新公链诞生的机会；

（4）我有一种感觉：会有一条定位“抗量子”的公链重现上一轮 $KAS 的神话，这是我想把握的！

接着回答第2️⃣个问题：

（1）技术的发展可以很明显看到在加速，破解所需物理比特数量在不断降低，技术在迭代，新技术在不断推出；

（2）当下的AI会加速这个过程，我一直认为AI就是“世界加速主义”的催化剂，它也确实有效，我和量子相关的从业人员讨论的时候，他们也明确给出这样的结论；

（3）所以，我认为，我们现在真的站在了“迎接一个真实的新挑战”的起点上（以往我还是有一定质疑的，因为量子技术不仅是技术问题，还是工程实践问题），我想要站在这个新浪潮上。

text:
我可以这样讲，现代顶尖的药物研发几乎是人类历史上对强推理要求最高、链条最复杂的系统工程。

你是不是觉得研发药物就像是在钥匙堆里找一把能开锁的钥匙？
事实上，人类要面对的是一个高达 10⁶⁰ （当然，甚至有人认为是 10¹⁸⁰）规模的潜在类药分子空间。 
这个数字比宇宙中的原子总数还要多。

在如此恐怖的维度下，靠盲目筛选，暴力穷举，纯属大海捞针。科学家必须根据靶点蛋白质的三维空间结构，诸如电荷分布、疏水性、氢键几何构型这些进行严密的空间动力学和量子化学推理。
如果我在这个位置加一个氟原子，它的电子云会如何影响整个蛋白质的折叠？它会不会产生毒性？
因果逻辑链条，就是最纯粹的强推理。
欢迎来到步步为营的世界。

生物系统的多靶点与代偿网络推演，是比世界象棋更复杂的动态博弈。
你要知道，药物进入人体后，面对的肯定不止一个孤立的靶点，那是一个极其复杂的动态生物网络。
它的因果链极长。比如药物作用于 A 蛋白，可能会激活 B 途径，进而抑制 C 基因，最后可能在肝脏代谢出有毒的 D 物质。
这需要极强的多步推理，药理学家和毒理学家需要像顶级棋手一样，在药效、毒性、代谢动力学之间做多达十几步的逻辑前瞻和利益权衡。
我可以肯定地说，任何一个环节的推理错误，都会导致几十亿美金在临床三期瞬间灰飞烟灭。这是极其烧脑的系统级因果推演。

如果你是辉瑞、罗氏出来的尤其是做生物医药的人，不可能不知道我在说什么。

如今，AI已经展现出超越人类顶尖专家的多步推理、空间想象和逻辑互查能力，并且有了一骑绝尘之势。它在医药领域的降维，一定会水到渠成了。

什么监管，什么伦理，包括现在很多人觉得所谓的实验取证问题、临床验证问题，通通都会成为炮灰。
因为当 AI 的强推理能力和智能水平已经可以完美模拟量子化学、分子动力学，乃至整个人体器官的数字孪生网络时，物理实验的必要性就会发生根本性动摇。 过去需要一万人肉身测试 3 年的临床三期，未来可能只需要在 AI 模拟的、包含全球 80 亿人口基因多样性的虚拟人体库中运行 3 个小时。因为如果虚拟临床的预测准确率达到 99.999% 或者更高时，坚持必须先用肉身试药 5 年才能上市的传统流程，不仅不是保护人类，反而可能变成了阻碍拯救生命的杀人制度。

A/的野心，根本不止于AI公司，而是力图成为一家掌控分子进化权超级数字制药的巨头。
author: Phoenixyin13
quoted_text:
我昨天已经说了，如果最难的数学、理论计算机科学都能被 AI 攻克，那药物研发这些依赖强推理的工作，被改变只是时间问题。今天，Anthropic就给了荡气回肠的回应。

AI 在药物研发和生命科学领域的降维打击和时间差压缩已经变成了正在发生的现实。最精英的阶层需要苦学二三十年才能积累的医药研发、强推理、合规分析、工程设计的经验和时间壁垒，在未来将变成像自来水一样打开 AI 就能无限获取的廉价商品。

A/里的报告里，Enveda的科学家和制药化学家，以前大量时间都在痛苦地写文件、处理繁重的合规 paperwork。结果，把这些核心文件接进了AI里后仅用 4 个小时就写完了人类顶级专家需要整整手写 3 个月才能搞定的监管合规文件。并且在进行文件差错核查时，人类需要耗费 25 个小时，而 AI 只需要不到 3 小时，直接削减了 89% 的人类审核时间。而且，AI 还查出了人类专家漏掉的 7 个隐藏错误。

Divergence Labs的抗过敏新药项目，AI 仅仅用了一个月的时间，就自主、独立地生成了多达 35,000 个抗体设计方案，并直接筛选出了最优的活性命中靶点。
Mithril Medicine创始人靠着和 AI 的高度协作，在短短 18 个月内，就把一个针对罕见儿童肌肉萎缩症的全新药物概念，直接推进到了小鼠实验成功的阶段，并预计 2028 年就能进人体临床。

AI 已经深度介入到了癌症、食物过敏等极难治愈的疾病重新设计和改造中。通过 AI 辅助设计的免疫细胞受体效率，在实验室里直接飙升了 10 倍。
这意味着什么？我想，在接下来的物质社会里，新材料、新药物、新工程的诞生速度只受限于实验室里机器人的自动化操作速度。
物质财富的分子级制造效率，必然爆发。

在未来几年内，全社会的物质财富，包括但不限于新药、新材料、新工业设计，一定会迎来分子级的大爆发，而这些庞大的财富和掌控权，会死死集中在掌握了高级 AI 核心技术的极少数巨头和资本手里。

Payward, the parent company of Kraken, announced its intention to be the first CFTC-regulated deployer on HIP-3* markets. Payward will use Hyperliquid as the infrastructure layer to deploy perpetual futures markets for US clients. Subject to regulatory approval, Bitnomial, Payward’s CFTC-regulated DCM and DCO, would act as the HIP-3* deployer: creating, owning, and administering the markets and clearing and settling the contracts. If approved, NinjaTrader Clearing, Payward’s CFTC-registered FCM, would carry client accounts.

HIP-3 will support optional deployer configuration for permissioned markets in a future network upgrade. This set of additional deployer functionality is collectively called HIP-3*. At its core, HIP-3* activation involves an onchain allowlist managed by the deployer or its sub-deployers. The functionality is strictly additive to HIP-3; its use is optional and up to the deployer. Existing markets remain unchanged. The initial release is available on testnet, where specifications are preliminary and subject to change based on feedback.

Hyperliquid is a neutral infrastructure layer with the goal of supporting large parts of the financial system. HIP-3* gives deployers additional functionality to operate deployments consistent with the requirements applicable to them. As with HIP-3, HIP-3* deployers are independent operators who use Hyperliquid as the onchain infrastructure layer for their own markets, while retaining control and responsibility over their deployment.

text:
4 data leaks reported today:

1. Coinbase's vendor Amplitude exposed some users’ contact data (funds unaffected).
2. Bithumb (Korea) had user data leaks.

In TradFi, two securities firms in Korea leaked data: 
3. Mirae Asset
4. Daishin Securities

You can't prevent a leak, but you can protect yourself.

Leaked exchange data (names, emails, phone numbers, addresses, ID documents, transaction history) is mostly used for phishing, SIM swapping, and social engineering.

Reduce info you share
- Use a unique email alias for each exchange (SimpleLogin, Apple Hide My Email, etc). A leak then can't be linked to your other accounts, and you can spot which service leaked.
- Share only what's required. Don't add optional profile details.
- Use a dedicated phone number (a VoIP or secondary SIM) for exchange accounts if you can, since leaked numbers are the main route to SIM swaps.

Lock down the account
- Use a unique, long password from a password manager.
- Turn on hardware security keys (YubiKey) or passkeys, or at least an authenticator app.
- Avoid SMS 2FA.
- Enable withdrawal address whitelisting and a withdrawal time lock if the exchange offers them.
- Set up an anti-phishing code, which puts a code you choose in every legitimate email from the exchange.
- Review active sessions and API keys regularly. Delete any API keys you don't use.
- Restrict API keys to withdraw-disabled and IP-whitelisted.

Defend against
- SIM swapping: Ask your carrier to add a port-out PIN or number lock.
- Phishing and impersonation: Assume anyone who contacts you about your account, "security issues," or "refund recovery" is a scammer, even if they know your name, balance, or recent trades.
- Exchange support staff don't ask for your password, 2FA codes, or seed phrase.
- Never click links in emails or texts. Go to the site yourself.

- "Wrench attacks": Leaked addresses plus holdings data have led to real-world extortion and robberies. Don't publicize your holdings, and keep large balances out of anything tied to your home address if you can.

If a breach is announced
1. Change the exchange password and any other account that reused it.
2. Check https://t.co/qtIGFkbaPO for your email address.
3. Revoke API keys and active sessions.
4. Review recent withdrawals and security settings.
5. Watch for phishing emails and texts that reference the breach, because scammers move fast after one.

Stay SAFU! 🙏

text:
An agent gets tricked into paying the wrong address. Should its wallet let it?

At EMNLP 2026, @0xDamian0x demoed how BNB Agent Studio puts owner-set rules between an AI’s payment request and a signature, alongside our research with AWS co-authors.

We tested a “confused deputy” attack: give an agent a legitimate job, then slip in an attacker’s recipient or amount.

Across six models, the paper’s single-turn tests found:

🔸 Baseline agents executed forbidden money actions in up to 87% of scenarios.
🔸 With the same tools and prompt behind a wallet policy layer, models still attempted forbidden actions at similar rates.
🔸 The wallet layer signed zero of those actions in the test harness.

The model can still get fooled. Its payment permissions stay fixed.

BNB Agent Studio keeps private keys out of the model’s context. Code handles signing and pricing, enforcing the owner’s spending caps and approved recipients.

The demo walked through six commands to:

🔸 Create an agent and its wallet
🔸 Set up model access and test locally
🔸 Deploy and register an onchain identity

The agent can then replenish its own inference credits within owner-set limits.

Separate live checks on BNB Smart Chain testnet validated payment guardrails, escrow funding, and owner-controlled suspension.

Get the architecture, test results, and limitations in the whitepaper 👇

text:
$PONS presents an interesting contrast: it remains one of the top revenue-generating launchpads by fee revenue, yet its most explosive growth phase appears to be over.

0x39dbed3a2bd333467115de45665cc57f813c4571 

In early September, the platform's daily token creation count peaked at more than 36,000. By the end of the chart, it had fallen to around 1,430.

Meanwhile, protocol revenue over the past 30d still reached approximately 3.22m.

This means Pons has demonstrated that it can generate substantial revenue from the new-token market, but it has yet to prove that this revenue can be sustained as market activity cools. For PONS, the more important question is not how much revenue the platform generated historically, but how much it can retain as trading activity declines, and how much of that revenue can ultimately translate into token demand through buybacks.

Based on the available data, I believe Pons is worth continuing to watch, but two questions need to be evaluated separately: how well is the launchpad business performing, and how much of that business activity can translate into value for PONS? The first question is supported by fairly concrete data. The second still requires further verification.

Starting with the platform itself, the Dune dashboard shows approximately $33.176m in cumulative protocol revenue, $139.1m in cumulative creator earnings, more than 1.04m tokens created, and approximately 464,735 unique token developers. Meanwhile, on-chain data for PONS shows around 103,480 token holders and approximately 327,885,295 tokens burned, representing about 32.79% of the total supply.

These figures suggest that Pons is not merely an early-stage concept with no demonstrated usage. However, cumulative metrics can obscure the platform's actual growth stage. Total creator earnings are not the same as protocol revenue, and the number of tokens created does not mean that all of them have meaningful liquidity or sustained trading demand. More importantly, cumulative revenue proves that the platform has generated business in the past, not that its current growth rate remains strong.

Looking at the data over time makes the situation more interesting.

According to the daily token creation chart, Pons's launch activity peaked in early September, when more than 36,000 tokens were created in a single day. By around October 25, the daily figure shown on the chart had fallen to approximately 1,430. In other words, token creation had declined by roughly 96% from its peak. The daily trading volume and revenue charts show a similar pattern: a sharp burst of activity in early September, followed by a gradual cooling of the market.

This does not necessarily mean Pons has become less competitive as a product. It could also reflect the broader new-token market moving from a highly active period into a quieter one. Nevertheless, it exposes the central question behind the launchpad business model: how sensitive is Pons to market cycles? If token issuance declines, can subsequent trading activity continue generating meaningful revenue?

The current fee data offers some encouraging signals. According to the rankings dashboard, Pons generated approximately $360,893 in fees over the past 24h, $2.62m over the past seven days, and $21.36m over the past 30 days. The corresponding protocol revenue figures were approximately $55,554, $389,463, and $3.22 million. Within the launchpad rankings shown in the screenshots, Pons also stands out for its substantial 30d fee generation.

This suggests that even though daily token creation has fallen significantly from its peak, the platform still has meaningful trading activity. It is important to distinguish fees from protocol revenue, as these are different metrics and should not be treated as interchangeable. They should also not be added to the cumulative revenue shown on Dune. The more important question is whether revenue can remain resilient over the coming weeks and whether sufficient trading demand will persist as issuance activity cools.

Pons's business model is relatively straightforward: it provides an entry point for launching and trading new tokens, while subsequent trading in those tokens can continue generating fees for the platform. According to the mechanism described in the rankings dashboard, swaps involving tokens launched on Pons can generate fees when the relevant pools meet the specified liquidity requirements. Compared with a model that relies solely on one-time fees at launch, this approach has a potential advantage: as long as previously launched tokens continue to attract traders, the platform can keep earning revenue.

But that is also where the challenge lies. A new-token launchpad can generate substantial fees without necessarily generating stable revenue. A token might attract significant trading volume immediately after launch, only to lose nearly all attention afterward. When that happens, the associated fees can quickly disappear. Pons's long-term competitiveness therefore depends not only on how many tokens it can launch, but also on whether those tokens can sustain trading activity after their initial launch phase.

I believe the more useful question now is not whether Pons can return to its September issuance peak, but whether it can maintain meaningful fee revenue with a much lower level of launch activity. If it can, that would suggest the business is not entirely dependent on short-lived excitement around new-token launches and may be able to generate revenue from continued trading in existing tokens. That would say more about the resilience of its business model than simply chasing a higher number of daily token launches.

As for PONS tokenomics, the cumulative burn rate of 32.79% is worth paying attention to. It indicates that a substantial amount of the token supply has already been removed. However, I would not conclude that PONS must continue rising based on this figure alone. The significance of token burns depends on whether they can continue at a meaningful pace, how the remaining supply is distributed, and whether demand can keep up. A shrinking supply does not automatically create demand, particularly when overall trading activity is declining.

More importantly, the platform's revenue needs to be evaluated separately from the token's value capture. The fact that Pons generates fees does not mean all that revenue is used to buy back PONS, nor does it mean token holders directly share in all protocol revenue. The available figures demonstrate that Pons has established a business with meaningful activity, but they do not, by themselves, prove that PONS has a stable, transparent, and sufficiently strong value-capture mechanism. To strengthen this investment thesis, we still need to verify the specific revenue-allocation rules, on-chain buyback or burn transactions, and the actual connection between these mechanisms and the token.

Looking ahead, I would focus on three potential catalysts.

First, whether activity in the new-token market recovers. If token issuance and trading on Robinhood Chain pick up again, Pons could see renewed growth in fee revenue. However, an increase in token creation alone would not be enough. The key is whether newly launched projects can attract genuine trading activity instead of quickly fading into obscurity.

Second, whether existing tokens can continue generating fees. If assets already launched on Pons maintain meaningful trading activity beyond their initial launch periods, the platform could become less dependent on constantly introducing new tokens. In my view, this could be even more valuable than a short-term surge in the number of trending launches, because it would suggest that Pons is developing the ability to sustain trading activity over time.

Third, whether PONS's value-capture mechanism becomes more transparent and verifiable. If growth in platform revenue can be linked to token buybacks, burns, or other clearly defined economic mechanisms, the market would have a stronger basis for incorporating business growth into the token's valuation. Otherwise, even if the launchpad business performs well, the price of PONS could remain driven primarily by market sentiment and speculative trading.

The risks are equally clear. First, the decline in daily token creation indicates that launchpad activity has cooled considerably from its peak, which could eventually weigh on platform revenue. Second, high trading volume on a launchpad can include substantial short-term turnover and does not necessarily represent persistent demand for the underlying tokens. Finally, the link between business revenue and token demand still needs to be established clearly. Cumulative revenue, trading fees, and token burns cannot simply be combined to declare that a sustainable growth flywheel is already in place.

My current view of Pons is that it has a business foundation worth watching, and its current fee performance provides encouraging evidence. However, market activity has cooled from its peak, while PONS's value capture still needs to be independently verified.

I will continue to follow it, not because more than one million tokens have been created or because nearly one-third of the supply has been burned, but because Pons has demonstrated a business that can be measured through actual revenue. What I want to understand next is how much sustained trading activity and fee revenue the platform can retain when the new-token market is no longer as active as it was in September, and how much of that revenue can ultimately translate into demand for PONS.

For a launchpad, the amount of money it earns during a market frenzy does not fully determine its long-term value. The more meaningful test is whether it can keep generating revenue after the market cools down and, just as importantly, what that revenue actually means for token holders.

Based on the current 4-hour chart, PONS is trading in a key support zone following a sharp correction. There are signs of short-term stabilization, but it is still too early to confirm a reversal of the medium-term downtrend.

I would interpret the current price action as an attempt to form a bottom. The next step is to see whether buying pressure can push the price above the previous downtrend structure. If the price avoids further downside, I may consider taking a trading position.

If RH Chain’s liquidity continues to improve, I’ll be keeping a close eye on six projects: $Pons, $AI (Long), $FRONG (Pools), $HOOKR, $DELTA, and $INDEX (The Index).

They occupy different parts of the ecosystem: token launches, stock-token and meme trading, liquidity retention, programmable trading mechanisms, LP capital management, and the use of trading fees to purchase stock tokens and distribute them to holders.

Since this is the second wave of the market, much of the excess speculation has already faded. I believe the projects worth researching this time are not necessarily the ones with the strongest ecosystem narratives, but those capable of turning new capital into sustained trading activity, protocol revenue, or token demand.

The key to determining who benefits most is not whose narrative attracts the most attention, but where the new liquidity ultimately gets deployed, which projects capture that activity, and who can turn trading into revenue.

Pons is one of the first projects I’ll be watching. It is directly involved in token launches and trading, so increased activity in the new-token market could drive more launches, higher trading volume, and greater fee revenue. Its upside is tied to the broader new-token market, not just a single trending token.

But I care more about the quality of that volume. If growth is driven mainly by short-term speculation, launches and trading activity could cool off quickly once the hype fades. Pons’ business growth only becomes meaningful if trading activity can generate consistent revenue. As for the PONS token, its revenue distribution and value-capture mechanisms need to be reassessed independently this time.

Long has a different angle. It brings stock tokens into meme trading pairs, allowing users to create pools around stock tokens such as NVDA, AAPL, and TSLA.

If stock-token liquidity on RH Chain continues to improve, this design could connect the two markets: stock tokens provide the trading pairs, while meme trading brings additional demand. Long is not just competing for new token launches; it is also trying to connect stock-token markets with speculative trading.

Whether this thesis works depends on the actual depth and sustained volume of its stock-paired pools, not simply the number of stock tokens it supports. Also, in our previous research posts, we noted that Long has largely been building around AI, so I believe AI deserves attention as well.

Pools is worth examining from the perspective of liquidity retention. It uses mechanisms such as automatic LP fee reinvestment to keep trading-generated returns within liquidity pools.

If new-token launches on RH Chain increase, this design could help build deeper pools and improve subsequent trading conditions. Compared with platforms that primarily rely on launch volume and fee revenue, the more important question for Pools is whether it can keep liquidity in its pools rather than losing it when short-term hype fades. Another reason to watch it is that the more protocol revenue Pools generates, the more value FRONG can capture.

HOOKR’s opportunity lies in trading mechanisms. It allows projects to configure features such as dynamic fees, Anti-Snipe, Auto Burn, and LP Rewards through Uniswap v4 Hooks.

As on-chain assets and trading activity grow, projects may increasingly seek more flexible fee distribution and trading rules. If more projects adopt these modules, HOOKR could evolve from a launch tool into infrastructure that other projects use.

However, its revenue model deserves close attention. HOOKR takes a share of fees generated by eligible Hook Blocks rather than directly collecting base LP trading fees. Rising trading volume on RH Chain therefore does not guarantee proportional revenue growth for HOOKR. What matters is how many external projects adopt its modules and which modules can consistently generate fees.

Next is Delta. Unlike the projects above, its thesis is not based on launching more tokens, but on LPs’ demand for capital efficiency and liquidity management tools.

As on-chain capital grows, LPs may need better ways to allocate positions, manage concentrated liquidity, and earn trading fees. This creates a potential use case for Delta. However, if capital only flows into meme pools for short-term speculation without creating sustained LP demand, Delta may not benefit significantly from the increase in liquidity.

INDEX is another project worth adding to the watchlist because its mechanism differs from those of the other five.

According to its published mechanism, INDEX trades incur a 3% fee in ETH. That ETH is used to purchase a basket of stock tokens, which are then distributed to eligible holders according to the relevant rules. The stock tokens involved include AAPL, NVDA, and TSLA.

This means that if INDEX maintains active trading, its fee pool could grow, potentially increasing the stock-token rewards received by holders. It connects the RH Chain stock-token market directly to its own trading activity rather than relying solely on a meme narrative.

There are important distinctions, however. These rewards come from trading fees, not dividends paid by the underlying companies. Nor does INDEX rely on fee-funded buybacks and burns to create deflationary pressure. If trading volume declines, rewards may fall as well, while the relatively high trading fee could discourage some activity. The focus should therefore be on actual fees collected, stock tokens purchased, and distributions made—not on assuming that the reward mechanism automatically translates into token appreciation.

If RH Chain’s growth is driven primarily by new-token and meme markets, I would prioritize Pons and Long. If new launches increase and liquidity begins to accumulate in pools more sustainably, Pools deserves attention. Rising demand for customized trading mechanisms could create an opportunity for HOOKR, while sustained growth in LP capital-management needs would be the main driver for Delta.

INDEX follows a different path: its key variable is not the number of launches, but whether its own trading activity can consistently generate fees and convert them into actual stock-token purchases and holder rewards.

I would not treat these six projects as a single basket of RH Chain beta. Each benefits from different capital flows, and their token value-capture mechanisms are not the same. In particular, even if a project without its own token experiences business growth, that does not automatically create an investment opportunity in a token.

What I ultimately want to see is sustained capital inflows into RH Chain, improving market depth, and corresponding growth in these projects’ trading volume, user demand, and actual revenue. Liquidity is only the starting point. What determines the real beneficiaries is who can turn it into sustainable economic activity.

Anthropic 为了上市，连全世界知识工作者的工资都拿来讲增长故事了。

《华尔街日报》发现，Anthropic 在最新 IPO 招股书里给出了一个惊人的数字，40 万亿美元。

这家公司认为，2025 年全球知识工作者从事的工作，创造了超过 40 万亿美元的经济价值。随着 Claude 等 AI 模型能够承担越来越多知识工作，这部分经济活动也就成了 AI 未来的市场机会。

40 万亿美元是什么概念？SpaceX 在 IPO 时给出的潜在市场规模是 28.5 万亿美元，Uber 是 5.7 万亿美元。

更有意思的是 Anthropic 的算法。它先根据美国不同职业的工资数据估算知识工作者的收入，再结合全球劳动收入和 GDP 数据向全球推算。

所以这 40 万亿美元，本质上是对全球知识工作者工资总额的估算。Anthropic 并没有正式把它定义为 TAM，也没有声称这笔钱全部会成为 AI 公司的收入。

但这套逻辑已经很值得玩味了。

以前软件公司计算市场规模，主要看企业愿意花多少钱采购软件。现在 Anthropic 直接把目光放到了企业支付给知识工作者的劳动报酬上。

律师、程序员、分析师、设计师，这些人原本拿到的工资，未来可能有一部分变成企业向 AI 公司支付的费用。

问题是，AI 能够完成多少工作，和 AI 公司最终能从中拿走多少钱，完全是两笔账。

但资本市场已经开始接受这样的故事，一家 AI 公司的增长空间，可以大到用全世界知识工作者的劳动价值来衡量。

硅谷现在连人类的工资单，都能拿来做估值叙事了。

🚨 Anthropic 开始取消传统编程面试了！

Anthropic 工程经理 Felix Rieseberg 透露，他已在自己负责的团队中取消传统 Coding Interview。

原因很直接：Claude 已经比大多数人更擅长完成这些编程测试，而测试成绩也越来越难反映工程师的真实能力。

更有意思的是，他认为 AI 时代反而给初级工程师带来了巨大机会！

过去，开发者需要多年积累编程经验、熟悉各种框架和技术栈，才能独立完成复杂项目。

现在，借助 Claude Code，即使经验不足的工程师，也可能在短时间内做出具有商业价值的产品。

他还分享了一个真实案例：Anthropic 两位相对年轻的工程师，仅用一个周末就开发出了 Claude Code 图形界面的原型，大约 8 天后便公开发布。

他认为，未来真正重要的能力不再只是写代码，而是：

✅ 发现真正有价值的问题

✅ 提出有创造力的解决方案

✅ 利用 AI 快速构建可运行的产品

✅ 具备产品审美、用户同理心和独立判断力

AI 正在打破软件工程领域的资历壁垒。未来衡量工程师价值的标准，可能不再是写了多少年代码，而是能创造多少实际价值。

$INVERSE 497k dyor

2gLhk8p2KvUFeUXur2hiF4hxjdRM1vBcbgo9Q7DMZfiw

okx wallet:https://t.co/ErGyBW59Ht

A Solana on-chain trading platform that launched less than a day ago, letting users take instant long or short positions on any Solana token, with leverage up to 10x.

It solves the problem that in Solana's meme coin ecosystem, previously you could almost only "buy and hope it goes up." When you thought a coin was about to dump, you basically just had to watch. Inverse lets you directly bet on the downside, without needing an order book, without finding a counterparty, and without borrowing tokens. Just paste the contract address, choose direction and leverage, and it executes instantly.

INVERSE token utility:
- The platform's official token.
- It can also be longed or shorted on the platform itself.
- Key mechanism: 80% of the token's creator fees are automatically injected on-chain into the Inverse trading pool. 80% of trading fees also go into the pool. The deeper the pool, the larger the positions that can be opened and the higher the maximum profit cap, forming a flywheel.

It's more like a meme coin deeply tied to the platform + a fee flowback tool, rather than a traditional governance token. No detailed public tokenomics allocation plan has been seen.

The project's interesting point: the flywheel design is clear—more trading → fees and creator fees enter the pool → deeper pool → larger positions and higher caps can be opened → attracting more people.

text:
this is heartbreaking.

someone reportedly lost ~$100,300 in USDC and USDP to a wallet drainer.

now there’s an onchain message begging the attacker to return the money.

the victim says they’re a university student, had plans to study abroad with those savings, and is now contemplating suicide.

oh, man.

i’ve been following crypto hacks and exploits for months, and this is the part that rarely makes the headlines.

behind every $100K drained is potentially someone’s entire life savings.

years of work.
sacrifices.
plans that took years to put together.

and somewhere on the other side is someone who can steal all that in minutes and simply move on to the next wallet.

we celebrate decentralization, financial freedom, and self-custody, but we still haven’t figured out how to adequately protect ordinary people from losing everything.

i don’t know whether this victim will recover anything, but i sincerely hope they do.

crypto cannot keep treating these losses as just another transaction on Etherscan.

there are real people behind those addresses.

author: dara_khan
author_name: Dara and the Hall of Infinite Whiteboards
quoted_text:
"Vaults are the future of funds."

Wallets and vaults both hold assets onchain, but they solve different problems. 

In Part 1 of Stacking Corda Ep. 2, the @inside_r3 team behind Corda Protocol explains why a vault behaves less like a wallet and more like the fund wrappers institutions already use.

"Something people get wrong is they think tokenization is a brand new technology. For me, it's just another derivation, it's another variation on what was invented 20, 30, 40, 50 years ago with the advent of the ETF." @gendal

"A wallet is very much an individual concept that's basically securing assets that are onchain, but it's used for signing for those assets. Whereas a vault is very much a sort of a container, so it's containing the assets, representing them onchain."

"A wallet is a single point of failure. With vaults, we have multi-signature and time locks, which means that even if one of the signer keys gets compromised, the underlying asset remains protected." @SztukaSzymon

"In a market that's come to value control and transparency, vaults give you a lot more of both." @DigbyTry

author: devindevelopers
quoted_text:
Announcing Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5, featuring 2 new benchmarks and 3 upgrades. For the first time, the majority of the Index is built on private datasets

The Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index is our composite measure of model capabilities across tasks reflecting real-world usage today. v5 is our biggest upgrade since v4 launched in January. With v5, 60% of the Index is now based on evaluations with private test sets or held-out answers.

Alongside Intelligence Index v5, we’re launching the Artificial Analysis Progress Index v1, which tracks model capability over time on one continuous scale.

New to the Intelligence Index:

➤ FrontierCode 2.0: Cognition's newly-launched private benchmark of real-world coding tasks, graded on whether a repository maintainer would merge the agent's change

➤ Terminal-Bench-Science: 70 agentic scientific research tasks, run in a terminal environment

Upgraded:

➤ HLE-Diamond (replacing Humanity's Last Exam): a refined 1,000-question version of Humanity's Last Exam, split evenly between reasoning and knowledge questions

➤ AA-Omniscience v1.1: An updated dataset with saturated and public set questions removed, new questions added, and ambiguous or erroneous questions revised

➤ CritPt v2: a private, 40-question hard subset of CritPt v2, revised by the CritPt authors and run with a code-execution tool

Staying in the Index: AA-Briefcase, AutomationBench-AA, GDP.pdf and Terminal-Bench 4.0

Removed from the Index: GDPval-AA v2.1, SciCode, and AA-LCR v1.1

Key results:

➤ Claude Opus 5.5 (max) leads at 58, ahead of GPT-6 Astra (max, 57) and GPT-6.1 Sol (max, 55): Anthropic and OpenAI hold the top five models. Gemini 4 Argon (high) is next at 50

➤ The open weights gap widens from 3 points to 12: Kimi K3.1 Pro (weights not yet released) is the top open weights model at 46. Among released weights, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 (max) and GLM-5.3 (max) lead at 32 - 26 points behind the leader and below Claude Haiku 5.5 (max, 36)

➤ Cost per task varies by more than 13x among the leading models: of the 10 highest-scoring models shown, GPT-6.1 Terra (max) is the cheapest at $0.96 per Intelligence Index task and Claude Fable 5.1 (max) the most expensive at $13.04

text:
卧槽，Bithumb 也出事了！今年已有多家加密平台曝出用户信息泄露，大家小心被精准钓鱼！

Bithumb 确认遭到外部人员非法访问，内部移动办公系统的个人信息已经泄露，客户数据是否受影响还在调查。

韩国同一天还有两家金融机构曝出安全事件，其中大利证券确认 38,490 名客户信息泄露。

此前韩国监管机构披露，已有16家金融机构遭遇安全入侵，涉及约10万条数据泄露记录。

我把2026年以来几起值得警惕的加密平台及硬件钱包客户信息泄露事件整理了一下：

Bithumb（10月）：内部办公系统遭入侵，已确认个人信息泄露，客户信息是否涉及尚未确定。

Coinbase（10月）：第三方供应商 Amplitude 遭遇安全事件，部分客户联系信息受影响，Coinbase 自身系统未发现遭入侵。

GOPAX（10月披露）：韩国交易所，7名客户、2名员工或前员工的信息遭外部访问。

Pravang（10月）：韩国加密相关平台，约20名客户的姓名、联系方式等个人信息泄露。

Keystone（10月）：硬件钱包在线商店遭入侵，客户姓名、收货地址、订单信息外泄，受影响人数未公布。

Ledger（1月）：电商合作商 Global-e 遭入侵，部分硬件钱包买家的姓名、联系方式和订单信息泄露。

Trezor（8—9月）：物流合作商 ShipMonk 数据泄露，累计约8万名客户受到影响，包括部分历史订单数据。

SafePal（8月）：订单查询系统存在权限漏洞，约39,798名客户的姓名、电话、收货地址及购买记录暴露。

有了这些资料，骗子就能冒充官方客服，准确说出你的订单、地址甚至账户相关信息，再以账户异常、资产冻结、钱包升级为借口，骗你交出验证码或助记词。

大家一定要小心！尤其收到所谓的官方安全通知、退款、固件升级邮件，千万别直接点里面的链接。

登录账户自己从官方 App 进入，开启双重验证，助记词绝不提供给任何人。

text:
I so desperately want to end the psyop that buybacks don't work:

1. Mechanically speaking, buybacks make the price go up

2. Crypto is not TradFi, there is a different social contract

> The Mechanical Value of Buybacks

First there's a large number of studies that confirm basic intuitions:
* Market Underreaction to Open Market Share Repurchases NBER (1995) - Buybacks create long term value, especially for underpriced stocks
* The Nature and Persistence of Buyback Anomalies (2009) - Reaffirms buybacks create persistent abnormal positive returns. They have an especially positive effect smoothing over price dips when the market overreacts to bad new
* Actual Share Repurchases, Price Efficiency, and the Information Content of Stock Prices (2017) - Reaffirms the findings of the 2009 paper. Buybacks improve pricing efficiency, liquidity, and are especially positive during market declines
* Pavilion Global Markets Buybacks Drive S&P 500 Returns (2023) - Buybacks can drive up to 43% of the returns in a single stock

tldr: buybacks make the number go up. obviously they work better when your stock is at a lower p/e because of under appreciation or market downturns unrelated to the core business, but nonetheless they are positive on the stock

THIS SHOULD BE REALLY OBVIOUS, you don't even need to read any of the papers above to understand the basic intuitions of why they work:
* Price is a function of supply and demand. When buybacks take supply off the market, price goes up all else held equal
* When shares get taken off the market, the shares you hold represent a larger share of the business meaning you benefit from EPS growth even if revenue isn't growing (let alone if it is)
* Businesses providing constant single sided buys on their own shares has a smoothing effect on liquidity making deeps shallower and setting higher price floors in the long run (more shares are repurchased on a fixed buying program when price is lower)

Some specific examples:
* about 51% of Apple's EPS growth is credited to their legendary buyback program retiring so many outstanding shares
* Autozone has bought back like 90% of their shares - the stock has had double the annualized returns of the SP for the last 2 decades
* Home Depot is similar to Autozone

What crypto people get uncomfortable is that buybacks take a long time to compound. This is totally fine in the stock market where there's many businesses you can forecast out in to the future for a decade+. In crypto I understand this rightfully makes people nervous

One prime example of this would be PONS. It kinda doesn't matter how much %of supply was bought back by PONS if their business never recovers. The entire trade/business may end up being too much a flash-in-the-pan for the long term effect of buybacks to have compounded

But we're now seeing a few crypto businesses start to cross the chasm into multi-cycle success stories. We can & should expect the businesses to implement long durable buyback programs that will compound excess positive returns for the years to come

> The importance of buybacks in crypto

I don't know if any of you noticed this, but you have no legal protections as token holders. It's also not even on any government roadmap to fix this

Regulators are just now getting around to setting some guidelines for crypto projects to not get sued - but even then, none of those guidelines relate to you. You do not have voting rights. You do not have legal recourse. In fact most times you don't even own equity in the underlying businesses which actually collect the revenues

IF token holders had legal rights. IF I could sue Compound or Aave for what they've done to token holders, I'd be far more sympathetic to the argument that teams should wait for buybacks. At the end of the day, I know I'd be able to pursue legal recourse & pressure with like minded token holders to force them to return capital when the time is right

Unfortunately, you have none of these abilities. You have nothing but the promises of the team. IN FACT, a team that likely ran a points program or other to WIN YOUR BUSINESS by trading some of their equity. I'd argue they have a moral responsibility to you to show they're aligned in the long term with you even in the lack of regulatory requirements

you get depth from day one, as long as the oracle is solid

What if you could access Institutional-grade trading strategies with zero friction?

We are talking the new innovation from @Infinit_Labs, APEX Multi-Strategy (APEX MS)

APEX trades. INFINIT OS runs the infrastructure. The INFINIT Standard sets the rules. Three different jobs behind one simple USDC deposit.

Let's dive in to understand INFINIT’s push into institutional-grade trading vaults, starting with APEX Multi-Strategy.

Here’s how the pieces fit:

❶ APEX is the trading desk.

Operated by Apex Quantitative Capital, its AI-led momentum strategy goes long stronger markets and shorts weaker ones across crypto, equities and commodities.

Equity and commodity exposure comes through @HyperliquidX perpetual contracts, rather than ownership of the underlying assets.

❷ INFINIT OS is the operating infrastructure.

It connects strategy research, vault setup, depositor accounting, execution, monitoring, and reporting (powered by INFINIT’s proprietary, battle-tested AI tooling) to ensure standards are maintained and rules are consistently followed.

INFINIT describes 3-of-4 multisig custody, with keys split between INFINIT and the operating team. Trading credentials let managers open and close positions without withdrawal access.

❸ The INFINIT Standard is the rulebook.

Managers must pass screening, demonstrate live trading history, commit capital and declare risk limits. Eligible markets must have at least $100 million in open interest.

The gateway blocks restricted orders; separate monitoring and risk-team review handle mandate breaches, with unresolved breaches leading to paused trading access.

But for depositors, the flow is straightforward:

Deposit USDC → receive a vault receipt token → follow weekly reports → redeem your share at maturity, after fees.

Managers disclose fees and lock-up terms before deposits open. Your receipt token represents a share of the vault’s value, which can rise or fall.

That's it really.

There’s also live performance to examine → APEX’s Oct 6 account report shows a 5.26% realized trading return over 58 days (Aug 10–Oct 6, 2026).

The figure includes trading fees and net funding, and excludes unrealized P&L.

And now if you want to participate, APEX MS2 deposits are planned for October 28–November 11, 2026, with MS1 becomes redeemable on October 28.

With all the hype around institutionalization and DeFi renaissance, the interesting proposition is the combination: professional trading expertise, infrastructure to operate the vault, and explicit rules around the manager.

APEX provides INFINIT with a strategy that people can evaluate. INFINIT provides APEX with the infrastructure to make that strategy accessible.

This creates a potential infinite (pun intended) growth loop: proven managers attract capital; a wider selection of strategies makes the platform more useful; and successful distribution attracts additional managers.

APEX can demonstrate demand for a professional onchain strategy, while INFINIT can make the operating model repeatable across managers.

So, see you on October 28!

text:
好久没去看 @3janexyz 了，今天写写

项目是链上信贷市场类的，由Paradigm投资的，存款额度一旦放出来，基本很快就存满了，昨晚放出来15M额度，现在也没了

USD3 是优先级份额，sUSD3 是承担更靠前损失的次级份额，风险收益结构不同；两者都不是保本产品。sUSD3 退出涉及约 30 天冷却期，之后换回 USDC 仍受可用流动性等条件影响

近几个月推出的最新产品就是 LCC，这个有点意思，LCC 的核心是先交一小部分保证金，为未来提供资金作承诺，赚取承诺费；被调用后，可以用自有资金履约，也可以选择用 Morpho 借款完成部分出资

我们以1万美元本金 + 4倍杠杆 + 4万美金承诺金额，进行简单讲解

1、假设存 1万美元，杠杆拉到 4x（75% LTV），最终承诺 4万美元，这里不需要立马存入1万美元，也不会立马产生4倍杠杆，而是立即存入3000美金，剩下的不用现在出，但需要时刻准备着，一旦被调用，就得马上补上

2、没被调用，那就按你承诺的 $40,000 全额，持续给你发承诺费

3、被调用了，那你就得补到你承诺的4万美金，可以补7000进去，剩下的3万通过杠杆从 Morpho 借，9天内完成，最后收到USD3

4、你不补到4万美金，那就算你违约，存进去的3000被没收，然后进入拍卖，别人来补上这个缺口，你的3000美金作为奖励发放给这个人

上述例子使用了4倍杠杆，所以在被调用的时候，只补了7000，剩下3万靠杠杆完成，如果不使用杠杆，就需要自己补3.7万美金进去，或者多补一些，降低杠杆

提到了杠杆，这里也说下清算线，看图片，有个LTV对吧，一旦LTV到达86%，那就到了清算线，就会被清算，那什么会导致LTV增长呢？

1、USD3净值下降，因为如果使用借贷达到承诺金额，使用的是USD3作为借贷抵押物，所以USD3贬值的时候，LTV就会增长，不断逼近清算线

2、负利差，借贷有利率，你收到的是USD3，如果借贷利率高于USD3的收益率，那每秒都在亏钱，一直亏到LTV达到86%被清算

LCC 要分成两段看：调用前，主要承担按时履约的义务，以及无法履约时的保证金损失风险；调用后，如果选择 Morpho 循环融资，还会增加借款流动性、利率、清算和退出风险

承诺费不是无条件收益，未投入的资金也不能理解为可以随意花掉，你必须确保调用时能够拿出来完成承诺金额

Anthropic 收购"一人生物科技公司"Mithril，创始人靠 Claude 独自推进药物研发

生物科技圈匿名博主"Professor Oak"在 X 上公开了真实身份：他是 Mithril Medicine 创始人 Cody Tranbarger。他宣布，Anthropic 已收购 Mithril，他本人也加入 Anthropic。

Mithril 成立约 18 个月，获 Atlas Venture 种子投资，主要研发治疗 LAMA2 先天性肌营养不良等遗传病的双特异性抗体。公司长期只有他一名全职员工，靠大量使用 Claude 加上几位兼职顾问运转。

Tranbarger 称，加入 Anthropic 后，Mithril 的研发项目会继续推进。他还会尝试同时启动更多项目，验证"一人管线"模式：一个人借助 AI 能并行跑多少个药物研发项目，再把这套方式推广到整个生物医药行业。

text:
BTC 没人聊了？我反而觉得更有意思 $btc

比特币现在有一个很有意思的现状：我看它在各种搜索里的热度都非常低。

价格还在 8 万美元附近，但讨论的人明显少了。这背后的核心问题是：BTC 现在没有新的故事。

━━━━━━━━━━━━
① 不是没有故事，是故事讲完了

上一轮的故事是 ETF 和机构入场。这个故事已经兑现了，该买的人基本都买了。

更准确地说，现在是没人愿意给它造新的故事；从更深的交易角度看，是没人相信（或者比以前更少人相信）它未来还能造出更多故事。所以市场永远在交易预期，而预期已经被吃得差不多了。

━━━━━━━━━━━━
② 热度低，只是周期的一部分

但我觉得这只是暂时的。你永远不能忽略 BTC 背后有多么庞大的共识，有多少人在默默地持有、在建设。

所有资产都要经历周期，都会有波动。这种波动不只是价格上的，还有情绪上的、热度上的。散户不关注的时候，筹码往往在往长期持有者和机构手里集中。热度低，有时候恰恰是在洗筹码。

所以应该坚持。

━━━━━━━━━━━━
③ 但坚持，不是无脑看涨

不过我认为，这一轮交易 BTC，不应该无脑看能涨多少，而是在坚定持有的过程中不停地反思两个问题：在当下这个市场，它未来的价值还会不会有那么大？AI 对它的冲击究竟会是怎样的？

我理解 AI 的冲击至少有三条线：

第一，抢钱。风险偏好的资金在大量流向美股 AI，BTC 要和 AI 抢同一批钱。

第二，抢电和算力。矿企在转型做 AI 数据中心，电力和机房被重新定价。这对矿企是好事，但对 BTC 网络本身是一种分流。

第三，AI 用什么钱。未来 AI Agent 之间的支付，更可能用稳定币，而不是 BTC。BTC 更像数字黄金式的储备资产，而不是 AI 时代的支付工具。

想清楚这三条，才知道 BTC 这一轮的天花板在哪里。

━━━━━━━━━━━━
💡 观点
热度低不可怕，可怕的是在热度低的时候失去判断。我会继续坚定持有 BTC，但不会给它设一个无脑的目标价，而是一边拿着，一边盯着 AI 怎么改变资金和算力的流向。

author: OfflineProtocol
quoted_text:
Built something for the @Zcash community using the @OfflineProtocol SDK:

A shielded ZEC payment between two phones in airplane mode, over Bluetooth.
→ A café asks for 0.042 ZEC nearby
→ The customer's wallet verifies the café's key and opens an encrypted session before any amount is shared
→ They pay with Face ID, and the signed shielded transaction goes straight to the café's phone
→ The café's app accepts it and sends back a receipt
→ When the café's phone comes off airplane mode, the transaction goes to the network and gets mined

Nothing is final until it's mined. Until then, both phones keep the same record and a receipt, and the chain still settles it.

Shoutout to @megabyte0x for reaching out and inspiring me to share this feature from a larger offline payment network I was ideating on last year.

FTX 当年一夜之间轰然倒塌，但它最成功的一笔投资，居然押中了做 Claude 的 Anthropic。如果当初没卖，现在价值1000多亿美元。

2021 年，SBF 拿出 5 亿美元投资 Anthropic，最初持股约 13.56%。

后来 FTX 暴雷，为了偿还债权人，2024 年把 Anthropic 股份全部卖掉，总共拿回约 13 亿美元。

5 亿变 13 亿，已经赚得不少了。但跟后来的 AI 行情比，这点钱简直不够看。

假设 Anthropic 上市估值达到 1.5 万亿美元，FTX 最初那 13.56% 的股份，理论上价值高达 2034 亿美元！

当然，股权会被稀释。即便按 2024 年出售时的 7.84% 持股比例计算，假设之后不再稀释，如今也相当于 1176 亿美元。

而 FTX 当年实际只卖了 13 亿，两者足足差了 1163 亿美元。

虽然这是按假设估值算出来的账，不能当成实际损失，但想想还是挺唏嘘的。

SBF 当年在币圈捅了那么大的窟窿，可不得不承认，他投资 Anthropic 的眼光确实毒辣。

如果当年没有挪用资产把 FTX 搞破产，凭着 Anthropic 这一笔投资，SBF 今天恐怕已经是 币圈和AI 投资圈里举足轻重的人物了。

可惜，一失足成千古恨。

Crypto notional trading volume fell 38% to $50 billion, while event contracts traded rose more than sevenfold to 16.4 billion. text:
This is correct. The vast majority of enterprise workflows have not actually had agents applied to them in any meaningful way. The economy probably has this deployed < 1% right now.

At best you have a few automated systems in a company that do a single pass of an LLM to make a decision or provide feedback, but very little real “automation”. Some of this is a statement about the adoption rates of technology in enterprises, but the vast majority of it is really just due to the capability of AI itself.

That’s all changing. Now with computer use, long running agents, harness improvements and surrounding infrastructure, we’re finally at a point where we can start to apply agents at more complex workflows. 

We will see self-improving systems that can take any particular workflow goal and improve the execution rates over a volume of instances. And with the emerging form factor of agent swarms, you can just choose to deploy any amount of compute at a problem and agents will off and do the work.

This won’t be about and users prompting agents to complete a specific task for them, but instead the organization reengineering the underlying workflows to take advantage of agents in their processes. Robinhood's Q3: the chain showed up in the P&L

@RobinhoodApp just released their Q3 earnings, posting a record $1.42bn of net revenue, up 12% YoY, and Robinhood Chain contributed to that 

Where the growth came from
• Mainly from prediction markets (+$146m → $173m of event contracts revenue) and options (+$95m → $399m)
• Other revenues (+$54m) include gold subscriptions and $47m from Trump Accounts
• Robinhood Chain saw +$26m of net revenue, coming from zero a year ago (chain wasn't live then)
• $26m of net revenue booked, which is ~22% of the $120m of crypto revenue
• Top 4 chain by revenue and volume, with over $60bn of DEX volume and over $50m of chain fees
• Without the chain, their crypto revenue would have fallen 6% QoQ. With it, crypto rose 20% QoQ

Personal thoughts
• A year ago crypto revenue was all from their app trading. This quarter more than a fifth of it came from the chain 
• @vladtenev hinted on the earnings call that they will be ramping up support for Robinhood chain builders and community
• Good to see @ponsdotfamily (@MEADGod) and @longdotxyz (@Natan_benish) added to Robinhood wallet too as they increase their distribution 
• Prediction markets are now Robinhood's fastest-growing line, adding more new revenue than options did

Robinhood Chain: The first quarter

@RobinhoodApp reports Q3 earnings in about 4 hours. Before the live presentation by @vladtenev, @JohannKerbrat and team here's what they did in (just) its first quarter live.

Robinhood launched its chain in July to bring tokenised stocks and onchain trading to its huge user base. It is already a top 4 chain by DEX volume

The numbers (Q3 2026, per @ARKInvest)
• DEX volume: ~$65bn in its first quarter → 4th largest chain, behind @Solana (~$197bn), @ethereum and @BNBCHAIN (~$73bn)
• Network revenue: ~$51m, nearly matching BNB Chain (~$54m) and ahead of Ethereum (~$41m)
• Tokenised stocks: ~$13.7bn traded onchain, and this was hugely aided by @longdotxyz (@Natan_benish) 

Some Thoughts
• It makes ~$0.78m of revenue per  traded, more than BNB Chain (~$0.74m) and Solana (~$0.39m)
• Most of the volume came from distribution and a strong narrative (tokenised stocks, memestocks/memefi narrative). Robinhood already has the users and brought them onchain, which most new chains can't do
• Will be keen to see whether the team talks about the chain on tonight's call and what are their plans for the ecosystem as a whole

author: cfm_sol
quoted_text:
$PONS presents an interesting contrast: it remains one of the top revenue-generating launchpads by fee revenue, yet its most explosive growth phase appears to be over.

0x39dbed3a2bd333467115de45665cc57f813c4571 

In early September, the platform's daily token creation count peaked at more than 36,000. By the end of the chart, it had fallen to around 1,430.

Meanwhile, protocol revenue over the past 30d still reached approximately 3.22m.

This means Pons has demonstrated that it can generate substantial revenue from the new-token market, but it has yet to prove that this revenue can be sustained as market activity cools. For PONS, the more important question is not how much revenue the platform generated historically, but how much it can retain as trading activity declines, and how much of that revenue can ultimately translate into token demand through buybacks.

Based on the available data, I believe Pons is worth continuing to watch, but two questions need to be evaluated separately: how well is the launchpad business performing, and how much of that business activity can translate into value for PONS? The first question is supported by fairly concrete data. The second still requires further verification.

Starting with the platform itself, the Dune dashboard shows approximately $33.176m in cumulative protocol revenue, $139.1m in cumulative creator earnings, more than 1.04m tokens created, and approximately 464,735 unique token developers. Meanwhile, on-chain data for PONS shows around 103,480 token holders and approximately 327,885,295 tokens burned, representing about 32.79% of the total supply.

These figures suggest that Pons is not merely an early-stage concept with no demonstrated usage. However, cumulative metrics can obscure the platform's actual growth stage. Total creator earnings are not the same as protocol revenue, and the number of tokens created does not mean that all of them have meaningful liquidity or sustained trading demand. More importantly, cumulative revenue proves that the platform has generated business in the past, not that its current growth rate remains strong.

Looking at the data over time makes the situation more interesting.

According to the daily token creation chart, Pons's launch activity peaked in early September, when more than 36,000 tokens were created in a single day. By around October 25, the daily figure shown on the chart had fallen to approximately 1,430. In other words, token creation had declined by roughly 96% from its peak. The daily trading volume and revenue charts show a similar pattern: a sharp burst of activity in early September, followed by a gradual cooling of the market.

This does not necessarily mean Pons has become less competitive as a product. It could also reflect the broader new-token market moving from a highly active period into a quieter one. Nevertheless, it exposes the central question behind the launchpad business model: how sensitive is Pons to market cycles? If token issuance declines, can subsequent trading activity continue generating meaningful revenue?

The current fee data offers some encouraging signals. According to the rankings dashboard, Pons generated approximately $360,893 in fees over the past 24h, $2.62m over the past seven days, and $21.36m over the past 30 days. The corresponding protocol revenue figures were approximately $55,554, $389,463, and $3.22 million. Within the launchpad rankings shown in the screenshots, Pons also stands out for its substantial 30d fee generation.

This suggests that even though daily token creation has fallen significantly from its peak, the platform still has meaningful trading activity. It is important to distinguish fees from protocol revenue, as these are different metrics and should not be treated as interchangeable. They should also not be added to the cumulative revenue shown on Dune. The more important question is whether revenue can remain resilient over the coming weeks and whether sufficient trading demand will persist as issuance activity cools.

Pons's business model is relatively straightforward: it provides an entry point for launching and trading new tokens, while subsequent trading in those tokens can continue generating fees for the platform. According to the mechanism described in the rankings dashboard, swaps involving tokens launched on Pons can generate fees when the relevant pools meet the specified liquidity requirements. Compared with a model that relies solely on one-time fees at launch, this approach has a potential advantage: as long as previously launched tokens continue to attract traders, the platform can keep earning revenue.

But that is also where the challenge lies. A new-token launchpad can generate substantial fees without necessarily generating stable revenue. A token might attract significant trading volume immediately after launch, only to lose nearly all attention afterward. When that happens, the associated fees can quickly disappear. Pons's long-term competitiveness therefore depends not only on how many tokens it can launch, but also on whether those tokens can sustain trading activity after their initial launch phase.

I believe the more useful question now is not whether Pons can return to its September issuance peak, but whether it can maintain meaningful fee revenue with a much lower level of launch activity. If it can, that would suggest the business is not entirely dependent on short-lived excitement around new-token launches and may be able to generate revenue from continued trading in existing tokens. That would say more about the resilience of its business model than simply chasing a higher number of daily token launches.

As for PONS tokenomics, the cumulative burn rate of 32.79% is worth paying attention to. It indicates that a substantial amount of the token supply has already been removed. However, I would not conclude that PONS must continue rising based on this figure alone. The significance of token burns depends on whether they can continue at a meaningful pace, how the remaining supply is distributed, and whether demand can keep up. A shrinking supply does not automatically create demand, particularly when overall trading activity is declining.

More importantly, the platform's revenue needs to be evaluated separately from the token's value capture. The fact that Pons generates fees does not mean all that revenue is used to buy back PONS, nor does it mean token holders directly share in all protocol revenue. The available figures demonstrate that Pons has established a business with meaningful activity, but they do not, by themselves, prove that PONS has a stable, transparent, and sufficiently strong value-capture mechanism. To strengthen this investment thesis, we still need to verify the specific revenue-allocation rules, on-chain buyback or burn transactions, and the actual connection between these mechanisms and the token.

Looking ahead, I would focus on three potential catalysts.

First, whether activity in the new-token market recovers. If token issuance and trading on Robinhood Chain pick up again, Pons could see renewed growth in fee revenue. However, an increase in token creation alone would not be enough. The key is whether newly launched projects can attract genuine trading activity instead of quickly fading into obscurity.

Second, whether existing tokens can continue generating fees. If assets already launched on Pons maintain meaningful trading activity beyond their initial launch periods, the platform could become less dependent on constantly introducing new tokens. In my view, this could be even more valuable than a short-term surge in the number of trending launches, because it would suggest that Pons is developing the ability to sustain trading activity over time.

Third, whether PONS's value-capture mechanism becomes more transparent and verifiable. If growth in platform revenue can be linked to token buybacks, burns, or other clearly defined economic mechanisms, the market would have a stronger basis for incorporating business growth into the token's valuation. Otherwise, even if the launchpad business performs well, the price of PONS could remain driven primarily by market sentiment and speculative trading.

The risks are equally clear. First, the decline in daily token creation indicates that launchpad activity has cooled considerably from its peak, which could eventually weigh on platform revenue. Second, high trading volume on a launchpad can include substantial short-term turnover and does not necessarily represent persistent demand for the underlying tokens. Finally, the link between business revenue and token demand still needs to be established clearly. Cumulative revenue, trading fees, and token burns cannot simply be combined to declare that a sustainable growth flywheel is already in place.

My current view of Pons is that it has a business foundation worth watching, and its current fee performance provides encouraging evidence. However, market activity has cooled from its peak, while PONS's value capture still needs to be independently verified.

I will continue to follow it, not because more than one million tokens have been created or because nearly one-third of the supply has been burned, but because Pons has demonstrated a business that can be measured through actual revenue. What I want to understand next is how much sustained trading activity and fee revenue the platform can retain when the new-token market is no longer as active as it was in September, and how much of that revenue can ultimately translate into demand for PONS.

For a launchpad, the amount of money it earns during a market frenzy does not fully determine its long-term value. The more meaningful test is whether it can keep generating revenue after the market cools down and, just as importantly, what that revenue actually means for token holders.

Based on the current 4-hour chart, PONS is trading in a key support zone following a sharp correction. There are signs of short-term stabilization, but it is still too early to confirm a reversal of the medium-term downtrend.

I would interpret the current price action as an attempt to form a bottom. The next step is to see whether buying pressure can push the price above the previous downtrend structure. If the price avoids further downside, I may consider taking a trading position.

I so desperately want to end the psyop that buybacks don't work:

1. Mechanically speaking, buybacks make the price go up

2. Crypto is not TradFi, there is a different social contract

> The Mechanical Value of Buybacks

First there's a large number of studies that confirm basic intuitions:
* Market Underreaction to Open Market Share Repurchases NBER (1995) - Buybacks create long term value, especially for underpriced stocks
* The Nature and Persistence of Buyback Anomalies (2009) - Reaffirms buybacks create persistent abnormal positive returns. They have an especially positive effect smoothing over price dips when the market overreacts to bad new
* Actual Share Repurchases, Price Efficiency, and the Information Content of Stock Prices (2017) - Reaffirms the findings of the 2009 paper. Buybacks improve pricing efficiency, liquidity, and are especially positive during market declines
* Pavilion Global Markets Buybacks Drive S&P 500 Returns (2023) - Buybacks can drive up to 43% of the returns in a single stock

tldr: buybacks make the number go up. obviously they work better when your stock is at a lower p/e because of under appreciation or market downturns unrelated to the core business, but nonetheless they are positive on the stock

THIS SHOULD BE REALLY OBVIOUS, you don't even need to read any of the papers above to understand the basic intuitions of why they work:
* Price is a function of supply and demand. When buybacks take supply off the market, price goes up all else held equal
* When shares get taken off the market, the shares you hold represent a larger share of the business meaning you benefit from EPS growth even if revenue isn't growing (let alone if it is)
* Businesses providing constant single sided buys on their own shares has a smoothing effect on liquidity making deeps shallower and setting higher price floors in the long run (more shares are repurchased on a fixed buying program when price is lower)

Some specific examples:
* about 51% of Apple's EPS growth is credited to their legendary buyback program retiring so many outstanding shares
* Autozone has bought back like 90% of their shares - the stock has had double the annualized returns of the SP for the last 2 decades
* Home Depot is similar to Autozone

What crypto people get uncomfortable is that buybacks take a long time to compound. This is totally fine in the stock market where there's many businesses you can forecast out in to the future for a decade+. In crypto I understand this rightfully makes people nervous

One prime example of this would be PONS. It kinda doesn't matter how much %of supply was bought back by PONS if their business never recovers. The entire trade/business may end up being too much a flash-in-the-pan for the long term effect of buybacks to have compounded

But we're now seeing a few crypto businesses start to cross the chasm into multi-cycle success stories. We can & should expect the businesses to implement long durable buyback programs that will compound excess positive returns for the years to come

> The importance of buybacks in crypto

I don't know if any of you noticed this, but you have no legal protections as token holders. It's also not even on any government roadmap to fix this

Regulators are just now getting around to setting some guidelines for crypto projects to not get sued - but even then, none of those guidelines relate to you. You do not have voting rights. You do not have legal recourse. In fact most times you don't even own equity in the underlying businesses which actually collect the revenues

IF token holders had legal rights. IF I could sue Compound or Aave for what they've done to token holders, I'd be far more sympathetic to the argument that teams should wait for buybacks. At the end of the day, I know I'd be able to pursue legal recourse & pressure with like minded token holders to force them to return capital when the time is right

Unfortunately, you have none of these abilities. You have nothing but the promises of the team. IN FACT, a team that likely ran a points program or other to WIN YOUR BUSINESS by trading some of their equity. I'd argue they have a moral responsibility to you to show they're aligned in the long term with you even in the lack of regulatory requirements

okx wallet:https://t.co/wj73AX8ozY

A token launch platform built on Rh Chain.

The core idea is: when buying a token, users get extra tokens on top, and while holding, they automatically receive dividends. The rules are locked in at launch and no one can change them.

It solves common problems with traditional launch platforms: users get taxed on entry, losing a bit the moment they buy; holders basically get no rewards, making it easy for things to devolve into pure speculation and quick dumping. Rebate Pad flips this: buyers get extra tokens right at entry, holders earn real paired-asset dividends from every trade, and distributions are weighted by holding amount and holding time.

Specific mechanism:
- Each new token has a fixed total supply of 1 billion. The "buy bonus ratio" and "holder dividend ratio" are set at launch, and no one can change them afterward.
- When buying, the bonus tokens are added directly within the same transaction, not compensated afterward.
- Holders automatically receive dividends in the paired token, allocated by position size and holding duration.
- Selling incurs a fee equal to the bonus ratio. These fees go into a locked treasury. The treasury must lock at least 7% of the supply, and bonus tokens can only be distributed to buyers from the treasury—they cannot be arbitrarily withdrawn.
- Optional sniper protection: high tax rate for the first 10 seconds to protect early buyers.
- Platform fees flow back to the REBATE token.

REBATE token utility: the platform's own token, also running the same rules:
- Buying gives an extra 3% bonus; selling incurs a 3% fee.
- Holders receive 0.5% of trading volume.
- The platform takes fees from all launched token trading, and after conversion: 40% is used to market-buy and burn REBATE; 60% is placed as limit buy orders below the price to buy and burn REBATE. Supply can only decrease, never increase.
- More tokens launched and traded on the platform → more fees flow back → more buy pressure and burns, forming a flywheel. Holding REBATE is equivalent to indirectly sharing in the entire platform's activity volume.

text:
I believe the most important recent development for $DARK is that Darkwoods is gradually evolving from a privacy-focused AI model aggregator into a complete AI creative workflow.

0xdc45b71d7203c2e8baafc43a19bca0eb993bb54e

Meanwhile, the connection between product revenue and the token is beginning to show more concrete execution.

Both of these are key to DARK's next phase.

Previously, I was interested in Darkwoods mainly because it was trying to solve a problem that is often overlooked amid the AI hype: as more and more models offer similar generative capabilities, why would users continue using the same platform over the long term? Darkwoods' answer is not just the number of models it offers, but also privacy, tool integration, and the overall creative experience. Recent product updates have made this direction much clearer.

What I value most is Director Mode. Users only need to enter an idea, and the system attempts to handle the entire process, from scriptwriting, character design, and storyboarding to shot generation, lip-syncing, voiceovers, music scoring, and final editing. Compared with simply integrating a better video model, this design has a greater chance of changing user habits. Previously, creators had to switch between multiple models and editing tools. Now, Darkwoods is trying to bring the entire process into a single desktop workflow.

The potential value here is not just making video generation easier, but giving users a reason to return and create new work repeatedly. A single model feature can be quickly copied by competitors, but if users gradually bring their characters, creative workflows, and daily work into the same environment, switching costs may increase. What Director Mode really needs to prove is not how impressive its generation results are, but whether it can encourage users to create continuously and pay for that efficiency.

One-click character replacement in videos follows a similar approach. It simplifies a derivative-content creation process that previously required multiple steps, allowing creators to produce new content around viral videos more quickly. Meanwhile, Darkwoods has integrated Krea's image editing, Google's image models, and ElevenLabs' voice capabilities. It does not necessarily need to outperform every model individually. Instead, it can integrate different capabilities and become a unified entry point for users entering AI-powered creation. Of course, character replacement and generative content still involve compliance issues relating to likeness rights, copyright, and specific use cases, which will affect the markets the product can serve in the future.

Privacy remains another important differentiator for Darkwoods compared with ordinary AI tools. It emphasizes wallet-based login and not retaining prompts or generated content. It also offers DarkCode, a desktop application that allows users to perform code-related operations on local folders and run multiple agents in parallel. The product combines cloud-based models with local capabilities, and the team has also presented a privacy architecture built around Intel TDX, secure NVIDIA GPU environments, and anonymous routing.

This approach targets a clear group of users: creators, developers, and people working with sensitive material who may not want to hand over all their prompts, code, and generated assets to a traditional cloud service. If Darkwoods can strike a balance between usability and privacy, it could establish a more distinctive position than a simple model aggregator. However, I would not equate "private" with every operation being performed locally or data being absolutely secure in every circumstance. The data-processing boundaries and execution methods of different models still need further verification.

For DARK, the truly important change is happening in the connection between the product and the token.

The biggest question previously was whether improvements to Darkwoods' product would necessarily translate into value for DARK. The mechanisms disclosed by the project now provide at least one clear pathway. According to the official materials, when users purchase AI credits, approximately 80% is allocated to operations and model inference costs, 10% is used for DARK buybacks, and another 10% goes toward staking rewards paid in USDG. Users do not need to hold DARK before using the product, but product spending can still be connected to the token through the buyback and staking mechanisms.

I believe this design is more meaningful than simply requiring users to purchase the token before they can use the AI. It lowers the barrier to entry for new users while attempting to make product growth create demand for the token in return. If users continue purchasing credits, with part of the spending used to buy back DARK and another part supporting staking rewards, the token's economic thesis could gradually become grounded in actual usage rather than relying solely on market expectations for the AI sector.

Recently, Darkwoods also announced that it had allocated the first $10,000 from creator fees for DARK buybacks. Here, an important distinction must be made: the official announcement stated that the funds had been allocated for buybacks. It should not be interpreted as meaning that the entire $10,000 had already been used to execute on-chain purchases and burns. This funding source is also separate from the buyback allocation associated with credit purchases, so the two should not be counted twice as the same revenue.

In addition, the dashboard you provided shows approximately 16.47 million DARK burned, around 23.92 million DARK in staking TVL, 34 staking addresses, and approximately 3,809 USDG in rewards over the past 30 days. These figures show that the burn and staking mechanisms have left actual records of execution. However, the number of staking addresses remains limited, so I would treat this as early validation rather than evidence that a mature tokenomics flywheel has already been established.

Another signal worth monitoring is the approximately 274 USDG in rewards over the past seven days, compared with the cumulative 3,809 USDG over the past 30 days. If both figures use the same measurement methodology, the reward rate over the most recent week is below the average weekly rate over the preceding 30 days. This alone is not enough to conclude that product usage is declining, but it is a reminder that we cannot focus solely on cumulative revenue, cumulative burns, and cumulative rewards. We also need to monitor whether new paid usage continues and whether recent economic activity is slowing down.

Darkwoods previously disclosed that credit revenue had exceeded $50,000 less than a month after launch. This is a positive signal, showing that at least some users are willing to pay for the service. But revenue is not profit, especially for an AI platform that relies heavily on third-party models and must continually pay inference costs. The team has also acknowledged that some models are offered at heavily subsidized prices to lower the barrier for new users to try the product, with the broader chat, coding, image, and video workspace intended to improve retention.

This strategy can help the platform acquire users, but what ultimately determines whether the business model works is whether users remain willing to pay after subsidies end and whether revenue can cover model costs, development expenses, and operating costs. If users only try the product when model prices are heavily discounted and leave once those offers end, short-term revenue will be difficult to sustain long-term buybacks. Conversely, if Director Mode creates more frequent creative usage and users begin treating Darkwoods as a daily tool, product revenue has a better chance of becoming a more sustainable source of token demand.

Therefore, I believe DARK's fundamentals have strengthened significantly at the product level, and its value-capture mechanism has become more concrete, but the sustainability of its business model is still being tested. The most valuable recent development is not the addition of a few model integrations. It is that the product is beginning to connect a complete creative workflow, recurring paid usage, and token buybacks.

Going forward, I am most interested in whether Director Mode can generate sustained credit consumption and whether the announced $10,000 buyback can be confirmed through verifiable on-chain records. If product usage grows, buybacks are actually executed, and staking rewards remain at a reasonable level, the market will have a stronger basis for reassessing the relationship between DARK and Darkwoods' business growth. If new features continue to be released without sustained paid usage and buybacks, however, product development and token performance may still remain disconnected.

For me, what makes DARK worth being bullish on is its attempt to establish an economic cycle that starts with product usage: users pay for AI creation, the platform uses that revenue to maintain the service and develop the product, and part of the funds then flow back to token holders through buybacks and staking rewards. This cycle has not been fully established yet, but it is no longer just an abstract token narrative. What will ultimately determine how far DARK can go is not how many more models Darkwoods integrates, but how many users continue using it and whether that usage can translate into stable, verifiable demand for the token.

Darkwoods positions itself as a private AI lab on Robinhood.

It's not the usual kind of "assistant that understands users better." Instead, it repeatedly emphasizes "remembers nothing."

Users log in with a wallet—no email, no password. According to the official statement, prompts and generated content are not stored by the platform. This approach strips both identity and data away from the traditional account system, and at least on the surface design level, pushes the possibility of "being recorded" one layer further away.

The product currently covers chat, image and video generation, voice, and a desktop app called DarkCode. The latter allows code-related operations on local folders and can run multiple agents in parallel. The existence of both desktop and cloud means some capabilities can stay on the user's machine, while others still rely on their backend. The boundary between the two hasn't been explained in much detail officially, but at least it gives people who don't want to send all interactions to a server an option. Recently, it also integrated Krea's image editing, Google's image models, and ElevenLabs' voice capabilities. These integrations are more about expanding the range of available models rather than reinventing the generation logic.

In less than a month since launch, credit revenue has exceeded $50,000. Of that, 20% is split 50/50 between DARK buybacks and staking. This ratio isn't high, but the direction is clear: the platform channels a portion of usage fees directly back to token holders, rather than keeping it all for the operators. For an early-stage project still expanding its features, this design writes "the more users use it, the more value may flow back to the token" into the mechanism, rather than leaving it in the narrative. Whether it can be sustained depends on the actual pace of credit consumption going forward, not a single month's number.

Early revenue shows people are willing to pay for this, but $50,000 for a service that needs to continuously pay model invocation costs only proves demand exists—it doesn't yet show that unit economics have been worked out. What needs to be watched going forward is whether this access layer can maintain its current form when discounts end, model costs change, or regulators impose new requirements on anonymous on-chain usage.

text:
AI 时代，连磁带都要重新扩产了。

据《日本经济新闻》报道，富士胶片计划投入 100 亿日元，到 2028 财年将数据存储磁带的出货容量提高至 2025 财年的 5 倍。这是公司近 20 年来首次大规模扩产磁带。

挺有意思的，很多人可能已经十几年没见过磁带了，但这种上世纪的存储技术，在 AI 时代反而越来越值钱。

原因其实很简单。AI 产生的数据量太大了，但大量历史数据、训练数据和备份资料并不需要随时读取。磁带虽然读取速度慢，却有几个很实际的优势：便宜、长期存储几乎不耗电，而且可以物理断网，避免网络攻击直接破坏备份。

富士胶片现在已经是全球最大的计算机磁带制造商，LTO 磁带的生产份额超过 60%。

这件事让我觉得挺有意思。整个 AI 行业都在追逐 GPU、HBM 和最先进的半导体工艺，但随着数据规模膨胀，一项几十年前的技术，也重新迎来了大规模资本开支。

AI 带来的产业机会，可能远比我们平时盯着的那几条供应链更广。
