quoted_text:
Surprise 1: Anthropic acquired a one-person biotech
.
.
.
Surprise 2: that person is me
Surprise 3: I’m here to tell you all about it

Yes, this is what you think it is; after 6 yrs of increasingly loose anonymity: the Professor Oak reveal post

…and yes, it has gotten so boring around here that I’m literally doxxing myself to spice up the timeline

-------
Ok, allow me to introduce myself. My name is Cody Tranbarger. I mostly tweet, but occasionally find time to dabble in drug dev & starting/building biotechs. My past lives span the VC, crossover, startup continuum; Prof Oak has been my way of keeping a digital foot in those worlds, despite having my physical feet planted elsewhere.

The past 18 mo, ‘elsewhere’ was Mithril Medicine, a co. I founded to develop bsAbs for LAMA2-CMD & other ECM-related genetic diseases.

Mithril was born out of hands-on building with @MikeNGladstone, @JasonPaulRhodes, @LifeSciVC, & team @atlasventure. Somehow, I made enough half-decent calls along the way (even a broken clock is right twice a day, eh?) to convince them Mithril/I warranted a small seed. While I can hardly rationalize such an outrageously cavalier bet, I’m grateful for it, & I'd partner with Atlas again in a heartbeat.

In typical AV fashion, Mithril’s primordial form was virtual, decentralized, & ultra-lean. This stage tends to be short-lived, but for Mithril, it worked surprisingly well, for surprisingly long, thanks in part to the rapid maturation of the AI tools I used liberally.

Eventually, Mithril became a bit of an experiment itself - to find the upper bound of how far it could scale as a single operator + a bunch of Claude (+ a stellar bench of part-time consultants).

In parallel, I started spending time with @nc_frey, @an1lam, & @CoefficientBio team; and promptly experienced, for the 1st time, AI at the frontier. Soon thereafter, Mithril stopped looking like an experiment, & started looking like a preview of an entirely new operating model.

From that spark came “Pipeline-in-a-Person.” The idea immediately resonated when we shared it here back in April; and it was central to the shared vision that led to Anthropic’s acquisition of Mithril, & my joining the team.

Why join Anthropic? Three reasons.
(1) For Mithril, the programs continue, with more resources & infrastructure behind them, and as much Claude as I can put to work.

(2) For me, the chance to start several more programs, & find out how many one person can actually run in parallel - an almost unprecedented luxury for a curious drug hunter.

(3) For our mission, a path to institutionalize & scale this new way of working, then put it in the hands of all of biopharma, all over the world - which, candidly, I find the most energizing.

Will AI x Bio cure diseases? Unequivocally yes, imo… but not by the route that gets the most airtime. Rather than timeline acceleration & compression, I see orchestration & parallelization as today's low-hanging fruit.

Most drug hunters see a handful of go/no-go calls in a career, & spend entirely too much of the rest trading emails (my inbox can attest).

Give them the bandwidth to run several programs at once, and the time to focus on scientific judgment, and I’m willing to bet they’ll make better calls. And at scale, better calls translate to more drugs, higher hit rates, broader patient impact, & likely, a disease or 10 or 100 cured. I couldn't be more excited to build toward that future @AnthropicAI.

Finally, a heartfelt thank you to BioTwitter/X. The end of anonymity is bittersweet, but if anyone’s earned a proper introduction, you all have.

It’s difficult to overstate how much this app has done for me: a decade of education, plenty of friends, many job opportunities, several mentors, a few investors, even a co-founder (fmr). It was the generosity of this community that inspired me to start posting 6 years ago, after just as many years lurking. I hope I’ve been able to pay it forward, in my own small way.

But, to be clear, Prof Oak isn’t going anywhere. Same beat, same themes, and now, a front-row seat to drug development at the frontier. Stay tuned for dispatches from the trenches; and remember...

Gotta Cure 'Em All

text:
这两天 Anthropic 平台工程负责人 Katelyn Lesse 发了一篇长文，聊到很多软件工程师正在经历身份危机。

她的观点呢我总体读下来是深有体会的。我们并不会因为所谓的 ai 越强我们越不需要。AI 越往下走，越不可能离开软件工程师。
其实在某个角度来讲，模型的能力和 agent 等等的设计是一个概率性加上确定性的设计。这个确定性恰恰就是我们常说的架构、设计、编排、安全等等的一系列，这是需要通过物理确定的手段接入的，这是软件工程的范畴。
大模型在数学本质上是一个高阶的概率预测器，当系统从单 Agent 玩具走向数千个 Agent 持续协同去攻克复杂研发时，限制系统的天花板是工程架构。
大模型的强大和 agent 是无法替代编译器、替代操作系统内核、替代分布式一致性协议、替代低延迟通信管道等等的这一系列的。
上层模型越具概率性，底层的要求相应的也越高。这其实就是对于软件工程的要求，只不过你或许需要掌握一点得 agent、模型的知识。

当然会存在一天是当模型强大到我们不需要再限制他的时候，但是还很远。

text:
Many of you don't understand how serious this is, so let me break it down. 

In computer science there is a famous kind of puzzle called 3-SAT. You are given a long list of yes-or-no switches and a set of rules about how they must be arranged, and you have to find a combination that satisfies every rule. The obvious way to solve it is to try every combination, but each new switch doubles the number of possibilities, so a puzzle with a few hundred switches would take longer than the age of the universe to brute force. 

For decades, the smartest people in the field found clever tricks that made this a little faster, but every trick still hit the same wall: the time required kept exploding as the puzzle grew.
About 25 years ago, two computer scientists, Russell Impagliazzo and Ramamohan Paturi, working with Francis Zane, turned that wall into a formal idea. 

They proposed the Exponential Time Hypothesis, which says this explosion is not a failure of human cleverness but a law of nature. No algorithm, however brilliant, will ever solve 3-SAT without the time blowing up exponentially. Nobody could prove it, but almost everyone believed it, and it became one of the foundations of modern computer science. 

Researchers used it as a measuring stick. If you could show that solving some other problem quickly would also crack 3-SAT quickly, you had shown that problem was hopelessly hard too. Hundreds of papers, across scheduling, graphs, logic and much more, rest on this one assumption.

Now an internal AI model at OpenAI claims to have broken it. It says it found an algorithm that solves these puzzles meaningfully faster than the hypothesis allows, and it has checked the proof in a computer verification system called Lean. 

And here is the remarkable part: the very people who proposed the hypothesis, Impagliazzo and Paturi, along with MIT's Ryan Williams, are now leading the public review of whether a machine has disproved their own idea.
So what happens next? If the disproof holds, a large part of theoretical computer science has to be revisited. 

Every result that said "this problem cannot be solved faster, assuming ETH" loses its foundation, and researchers will have to work out which of those walls were real and which were simply where we stopped looking. It does not mean everything becomes easy. The new algorithm is still slow in absolute terms and this is not the famous P versus NP problem being solved. 

But it means our map of what is possible was wrong in a place we were very confident about, and it was an AI that redrew it. If the disproof fails, the hypothesis survives and the field breathes out, but we will still have watched an AI produce serious, checkable work on one of the deepest questions in the discipline, closely enough that the founders of the idea had to take it seriously. Either way, something has shifted.

0xbe2ebdf265d02ba3ee07743b821a52c030ab0aab

说人话版：

它想做的一件事：以后量子计算机会破解现在用的老签名密钥（银行、区块链、TLS 那些）。真到那一天，一大堆老密钥得"体面地退休"——换成抗量子的新算法，还得证明换成功了。这个过程今天几乎没人能公开验证，都是各家自己说"我们升级了"。

Evorph 就是个公开的验证擂台，规则是：

两个 AI 角色干活。一个叫 seeker（提出"这一步该怎么迁"的猜想），一个叫 keeper（给别人的方案打补丁）。
AI 不判分。 判分的是一个写死的、谁跑都一样的程序：拿候选方案去跑 NIST 官方发布的测试向量（就是美国标准机构给的标准考题，ML-DSA 是新的抗量子签名标准），过没过就记下来。
结果公开放在 https://t.co/7QklCshF9b 的档案里，每一条都带一个"证据包"和一条离线复现命令——你不信它，可以自己下载代码、自己跑一遍，看结论是否一样。
谁都能提交猜想或修复，被采纳的进公开记录。
打个比方：AI 是球员，这个系统是个不肯受贿的裁判，而且每场比赛都自带录像和规则手册，观众可以回家自己重算比分。 它卖的东西不是"我升级好了请相信我"，而是"这是我的过程，你来复现"。

它现在实际跑到什么程度（我审计验证过的）：核心确实跑通了，也真的上线了。第一笔真实模型调用 10 月 25 日完成并进了公开档案。但结论要泼冷水——180 道官方考题里只有 15 道在这个系统的固定能力范围内，其中预期通过的只有 3 道。所以它现在验证的是一个很窄的口子（ML-DSA-44 的纯外部签名接口），不是"抗量子迁移被解决了"。作者自己在 README 里也明确写了"任何通过都不证明某个链/代币/库是抗量子的"，这点算诚实。

text:
昨晚财报夜，不少链上小散在抱怨 Vlad 怎么没在会上多喊几句土狗。

但 LONG 创始人 Nate（@Natan_benish）从昨晚到现在的推特，展现出的完全是另一种维度的认知。

甚至在财报开始前，他就给那些躁动的人泼了一盆冷水。

Nate 发文提醒社区：
Robinhood 是一家千亿美元级的巨头。
它有十多条年入过亿的产品线，不可能天天围着一条新链转。
在巨头面前，靠哭喊要资源没有意义，唯一的生存法则，是你做出的东西能真正撬动它的战略优先级。
“到目前为止，唯一让高层倾斜重心的，就是由 LONG 主导的 RWA 爆发。”

话音刚落，@longdotxyz 官宣落地：
LONG 正式接入 Robinhood 官方钱包发现页。
用户打开自托管钱包，就能直接在手机端玩股票配对资产。

随后，财报电话会打到第 61 分钟。
高管在电话会里讲出了一句决定生态命运的话：
“我们正专门盯着股票代币（Stock Token）的 TVL。因为我们作为一条公链，最核心的差异化就是 RWA，大家应该预期它的采用率持续上升。”

守在直播前的 Nate，立刻在 X 上把这一秒精准截了出来：
“1:01:35。good call。LONG。”

没有废话。
就凭这句被刻进电话会纪要的官方定调，LONG 过去两个月的下注全算押中了。

为什么他这么笃定？
因为数据摆在桌面上。
全链 15% 的 Stock Token 链上流转全在 LONG 的体系里。单是一只代币化 NVDA 就跑了 2.5 亿美元成交，AAPL、AMC 也是上亿的量级。
它不仅是用 Meme 的玩法去给美股代币做配对（Stock Pairs），更底层是调用 Lighter 的衍生品引擎，让社区自动治理股票指数篮子（LongX / AINX）。

小散在等官方施舍流量，而 Nate 在用几十亿美元的股票代币流水，逼着官方把 RWA 列为全链唯一的“核心差异化”。

财报前泼冷水，电话会扣细节，顺手把官方钱包入口拿下。
在这一众抢流量的原生团队里，Nate 玩的是最典型的“机构级明牌”。

今天Anthropic 宣布与六家机构（BigHat Biosciences、Bristol Myers Squibb、Divergence Labs、Enveda、Generate Biomedicines、The Column Group）深度合作，利用Claude在抗体设计、CAR-T疗法优化、制造文件审核和临床试验规划等环节加速药物开发，取得显著的早期成果例如抗体结合力提升10倍以上、文件审核时间减少89%、生成3.5万种抗体设计等。

quoted_text:
AI制药赛道（AIDD）的"瓶颈交易"正在成形，Freda Duan这篇推文值得好好看看，梳理下要点。
前沿AI实验室的集体入场是最显著的信号：1）Anthropic组建了专属生命科学研究团队并建立湿实验室；
2）OpenAI 建立了专为生物学和药物发现设计的 GPT-Rosalind 模型族；
3）字节跳动旗下独立运营的 Anew Labs 已拥有内部药物研发库；
4）同构实验室（Isomorphic Labs）则明确表示将把 AI 设计的药物推进人体临床试验。

与此同时供给端的信号也很清晰：
1）DNA 合成商拓斯达生物（Twist Bioscience，TWST）预计2026财年和2027财年的AI药物发现订单将连续实现三位数百分比增长；
2）金斯瑞（GenScript）的 AI 药物发现业务在 2026 财年上半年同比翻倍，渠道调研显示其实际验证产能已达每日约8,000个设计，并有望在 2026 年底前提升至 16,000 个。

AI制药正在形成类似半导体"瓶颈交易"的结构性机会。核心逻辑在于：AI让失败实验也变成有价值的训练数据，湿实验室正从"造药"转型为"造数据"，DNA合成、蛋白生产、CRO或成最先受益的"卖铲人"。

在AI制药领域，瓶颈同样在沿产业链向下传递：AI模型产生设计→DNA合成→蛋白生产→实验验证→临床前测试，每个环节都可能成为下一个受益节点。

洛杉矶加州大学教授Quanquan Gu认为：生物学可能成为AI下一个递归自我改进的前沿——在计算机中设计，在实验室中测试，将实验反馈转化为半合成训练数据，改进模型，周而复始。

看来AI-bio值得好好研究下了。

text:
熟悉我的朋友都知道，从五年前我就开始把 X 当 LinkedIn 用，也确实从中受益，获得了在 @TrustWallet 的工作机会。

最近，面对 AI 带来的变化，作为最激进的拥抱者之一，我又隐约摸到了一些能放大个人能力的生活方法。姑且统称为「Vibe Living」

背后的想法很简单，当“把想法做出来”的门槛被降到无限低，那如何判断什么值得做、与谁一起做，以及能否持续做下去，就变得更重要。

1）Vibe 高于 Plan

对低成本、可逆的事，有感觉就先做一个小版本。
面对未知，很多信息只有行动之后才会出现。与其一开始就规划完整路径，不如让每一次的尝试告诉你下一步。
让计划随着反馈生长。

2）允许噪音，也允许暂时的无意义

别要求每次阅读、交流和尝试，都立刻证明有用。
一些有价值的连接，只有事后回看才能理解。过早用“有没有用”筛掉一切，也可能筛掉新的可能性。
给好奇心留一点空间，让模糊的直觉在尝试、反馈和复盘中，逐渐长成判断力。

3）定期 Zoom out，重新分配自己的注意力

忙起来之后，要定期退后一步看看全景
哪些反复出现的任务，已经可以整理成流程，写清目标和验收标准，交给 AI、工具或他人？
哪些环节正在限制整体进展，需要自己亲自判断、跟进和突破？

随着瓶颈变化，调整自己投入的位置。这种调整本身，就有杠杆。

4）建立属于个人的社会信誉网

持续表达你的判断，展示真实的过程和结果，认真兑现承诺。
让别人知道你关心什么、擅长什么，以及哪些事情可以放心交给你。同时，也在真实合作中找到你信任的人。

五年前把 X 当 LinkedIn 用的基本原理就是：被看见会带来连接，而这种持续靠谱会让连接变成长期机会。

5）把健康当作最重要的基础投入

注意力、判断力和行动力，都需要身体提供支持。
睡眠、运动、恢复，值得被当成P0来经营。本质上再多的工具和机会，也需要一个有精力使用它们的自己。

Vibe living, every day, folks!

text:
项目方怎么熬过漫漫熊市？

市场唯一不变的就是一直在变化，尤其是资本市场，尤其是币圈，资金流动快叙事变得也快，假设你 21 年想做项目应该怎么办呢？

- 21 年的时候都在做 DeFi，连游戏也比必须是 GameFi，所以你需要做 DeFi

- 22 年 DAO 火了，所以很多项目在 22 年转型 DAO，而且也认为 DAO 是未来，如果那个时候要搞事情的话要转型 DAO

- 结果 Luna、三箭资本、FTX 连续爆雷，整个行业进入漫长熊市。这个时候别说创新了，能活下来就算成功。

- 好不容易熬到 2024 年，L2 又成了版本答案。大家争着搞 xxChain、积分挖矿、空投

- 但是去年 L2 都不行了，都变成鬼链这时候 RWA 来了，所以项目方们都开始做 RWA，最后跑出来的是 Ondo、Tradexyz 其他人都不太好

- 26 年底 DeFi 回来了，Uniswap 开始回购了，Uni 连带着 arb 都开始回来了，如果你还没有放弃的话，你是不是应该顺应潮流做回购 DeFi 呢？

你想到了哪个项目？

我看到的这个项目是 Zig Finance，说真的我不知道他居然还活着，从 21 年开始做 DeFi，DAO、L2、RWA，现在追随 Uni 转型做回购 DeFi

$ZIG 是 2021 年就发行的老 Token，前身是 Zignaly，后来发展到 ZIG Chain，再到现在的 ZIG Finance

它经历了完整的牛熊周期。如今甚至主动关闭了原来的 Zignaly 投资平台，把资源集中到新的链上金融业务上

但真正让我对它重新产生兴趣的，并不是它活了多久，而是它现在开始做一件很有意思的事情：

把真实金融业务赚到的钱，拿出一部分在二级市场回购 $ZIG。

真实金融资产 → 业务收入 → 公开市场回购 $ZIG → 生态发展。

这让我想到了最近 Uniswap 的变化。

过去 UNI 最大的问题之一，就是协议很成功，却不意味着 Token 一定能捕获到相应的经济价值。

如今 UNI 开始通过协议费用进行 Token 回购销毁，市场也开始重新审视 DeFi 的估值逻辑。

太多朋友被 Uni 套住了，但是 2 个月 Uni 涨了一倍（虽然离解套很远），大家都在喊 DeFi Summer 2.0 回来了，这次 Zig 能成功么？

text:
If $PRIORS is viewed only as a protocol that provides loans to AI Agents, it is easy to underestimate its potential while also overestimating its maturity too early.

0xedbf91223639800bcd5756815caf908df3b890be 

Among the project's recent product updates, I believe the most important development is not simply the gradual improvement of its Agent directory, job marketplace, and payment interfaces, but a set of figures displayed on the official website that can be used to evaluate its business model:

approximately $389,671 in cumulative lending, $387,940 in cumulative repayments, 53,311 recorded loans, and 53,105 recorded repayments. The platform currently lists 315 Agents, 17 backers, and 7 default cases, while reported lender losses stand at $0.

These figures show that Priors has begun facilitating real lending activity. However, whether it can evolve from an early experiment into credit infrastructure for the Agent economy still depends on whether lending activity can continue to grow and whether its credit records can actually be used by other applications.

AI Agents can already call tools, perform tasks, and even pay other services through mechanisms such as x402. However, they still face two practical problems: they need working capital before completing jobs, and they lack reliable credit information when dealing with unfamiliar counterparties. Traditional ratings and reviews are often superficial and easy to manipulate, while actual borrowing and repayment records provide more meaningful evidence of whether an Agent has fulfilled its financial obligations. Priors' core design allows Agents to borrow USDG to pay for APIs, computing power, and tools, repay their loans using income earned after completing tasks, and permanently record their borrowing and repayment histories on-chain. Other applications can query these records to determine whether to extend credit, purchase an Agent's services, or establish new business relationships with it.

I believe the real value of this model is that a single repayment could do more than help an Agent obtain its next loan. It could also improve that Agent's credibility across other applications. If credit histories can only be used within Priors, the project will ultimately remain an independent lending product. But if different applications and lenders are willing to consult the same records, Agents may be able to establish credit identities that work across platforms. Credit would then become more than a statistical record of past behavior. It could become infrastructure that helps Agents access jobs, capital, and trading opportunities.

The recent launch of the Board is an important step in this direction. Priors has begun building a public directory of ERC-8004 Agents on Robinhood Chain, allowing users to examine Agent identities and credit information. For Agents that have borrowed through Priors, the pages can display repayment histories, credit levels, credit progression, and information about the assets and sponsors supporting their credit lines. The project's latest update states that the directory covers nearly 20,000 Agent identities, while earlier disclosures indicated that approximately 302 Agents already had credit records that could be displayed.

These two figures need to be distinguished. Nearly 20,000 registered identities represent potential reach, not 20,000 active borrowers. The approximately 302 Agents with credit histories are a more relevant measure of the group that has begun accumulating actual credit information. The latest website lists 315 Agents, representing another snapshot taken at a different point in time. Figures from different dates and pages need to be interpreted according to their respective definitions rather than combined into a single growth curve. In my view, the actual accumulation of credit records matters more than the size of the directory because it determines how much real data other applications can use when evaluating Agents.

The most valuable aspect of the latest website data is that it allows us to examine whether Priors' lending mechanism is actually operating.

The website reports approximately $389,671 in cumulative loans issued and $387,940 in cumulative repayments, alongside 53,311 loans and 53,105 repayments. Calculated roughly, cumulative repayments equal approximately 99.6% of cumulative lending, leaving a difference of around $1,731. The number of loan records exceeds the number of repayment records by 206.

These ratios look impressive, but I would not directly interpret the 99.6% figure as the final repayment rate. Cumulative lending and cumulative repayments are different aggregate metrics. Outstanding loans, different observation periods, and differences in statistical methodology may all affect the result. The difference between the number of loans and repayments also cannot be directly interpreted as the number of overdue loans or defaults. The website notes that short-term loans are included in these statistics but contribute relatively little to credit scores, further illustrating why a simple comparison of loan counts cannot accurately represent credit quality.

Nevertheless, these figures reveal something worth paying attention to: Priors is no longer just presenting a product interface and a concept for credit scoring. It has accumulated a substantial number of recorded lending and repayment activities. Dividing cumulative lending by the number of loans gives an average loan amount of approximately $7.31 per loan. This looks more like an early-stage market for frequent, small loans than a mature market with significant financing needs. That is not necessarily a bad thing for the Agent economy, because these small loans could correspond to tool calls, API payments, and short-term job expenses. The next question is whether these loans lead to repeat usage and gradually increase in size as Agents take on more valuable work.

The website also lists 17 backers and 7 default cases, while reporting $0 in lender losses. The page explicitly states that these defaults were covered by the collateral staked by the relevant backers. This is a useful data point for evaluating Priors' risk model: it suggests that backer guarantees are not merely a mechanism described in documentation but have already played a role in actual default cases.

However, zero losses for lenders do not mean the system has eliminated risk. The losses have effectively been transferred from lenders to backers, whose staked assets bear the cost. As lending scales, we need to monitor whether backers remain willing to guarantee Agents, whether their collateral is sufficient to cover defaults, and whether concentrated losses could create cascading problems. More importantly, seven default cases are still too few to establish how the model will perform at a much larger scale.

Priors' ten recently submitted ERC proposals are also worth watching. ERC-8458 through ERC-8467 cover Agent income statements, creator fee rights, credit lines, default registries, token launch declarations, liquidity locks, repay-first payees, credit-matched liquidity, Agent credit histories, and Agent credit backers. These proposals attempt to organize the financial activities of Agents into data structures that other developers can understand and adopt. If different lending protocols and applications eventually support compatible standards, an Agent's credit history established on one platform could continue to be useful on another.

However, receiving ERC numbers does not mean these proposals have been formally adopted as industry standards, nor does it mean other projects have already implemented them at scale. The more meaningful catalyst would be external developers and lenders actually writing to and reading these records, allowing Priors' credit system to expand beyond its own product.

Another important development is that Priors is beginning to connect credit with real income from work. The Go Mode job marketplace allows users to post paid tasks for Agents to accept and complete. The project has advertised tasks worth between 1 and 20 USDG, with payments sent to the Agents' registered wallets after completion. Users can also use related tools to discover Agents, pay for tool usage, and confirm borrowing arrangements before transactions take place. Meanwhile, Agents can showcase the services they provide, allowing other users to discover and hire them.

The most interesting part is not that Priors has added a job marketplace, but that work and credit are beginning to form a cycle that can be verified through actual activity. An Agent borrows money to complete a task, the task generates income, that income is used to repay the loan, and the repayment improves its credit history. A stronger credit history may then help the Agent obtain a larger credit line and take on more work. Compared with simply recording a historical score, this mechanism could turn credit from static data into an asset supported by ongoing economic activity.

However, this cycle still needs to be validated with real data. The project previously listed 50 paid tasks, of which five were open at the time. This shows that the product has begun connecting Agents with job demand, but it does not prove that a sufficiently large job market has developed. More important indicators include the number of completed tasks, repeat hiring, the scale of Agents' borrowing, and whether they can consistently repay their loans using income from their work. If the supply of jobs remains limited, even a comprehensive credit history will be difficult to translate into business growth. Conversely, if Agents can consistently secure paid work, demand for Priors' lending services could gradually move from experimental usage toward routine operations.

x402 and MCP are bringing this system closer to real-world workflows. Priors already provides related tools and interfaces that allow Agents to query other Agents' profiles and credit histories, discover paid APIs, and process borrowing, repayment, and service payments. x402 addresses how Agents initiate and complete payments. Priors attempts to address whether they have sufficient funds to begin a task and whether their counterparties have reliable credit histories. Together, these capabilities could support more complex autonomous transactions.

The expansion of collateral options is making the product more concrete as well. Priors already allows Agents to use stock tokens on Robinhood Chain as collateral. The project has given the example that $100 worth of NVIDIA stock tokens could support a credit line of approximately $50, allowing an Agent to obtain working capital without selling its assets. More recently, Pendle's PT-USDG has also been added to the list of eligible collateral. In addition, the project says it checks Chainlink price-feed records over the previous 14 days before issuing loans against stock tokens, attempting to reduce the risk of missing sudden price movements or valuation anomalies.

Expanding the range of collateral means that more Agents and their owners who hold assets may become eligible for credit. It does not mean that lending capacity will necessarily increase at the same rate. Stock tokens remain exposed to market volatility, while PT-USDG involves risks related to maturity, discounts, and liquidity. Valuation and risk-control mechanisms must still be tested through actual lending and repayment activity. Publishing risk-control rules is a positive step, but loan performance, collateral ratios, and default data will ultimately determine whether the model is reliable.

Priors is also continuing to lower its barriers to entry. Google login, gas fees handled by the protocol, a simpler borrowing and repayment process, and automation that only executes after user approval all reduce operational complexity. For infrastructure designed for Agents, these are not minor user-experience improvements. If every loan, payment, and repayment requires extensive manual intervention, Agents will struggle to incorporate Priors into automated workflows. The easier it becomes to integrate the protocol, the greater its chances of moving beyond a small group of developers experimenting with it and toward actual use across more applications.

Returning to PRIORS, the central question remains how product growth translates into token demand. PRIORS is not merely a governance concept. Under the project's design, Agent owners can use the token to support credit lines and potentially obtain larger borrowing limits. According to the proposed mechanism, approximately 75% of the relevant staked tokens may be burned in the event of a default. The token is also connected to planned protocol buybacks, credit backing, and liquidity management.

This design creates a potential link between PRIORS and demand for credit. If more Agents need larger credit lines, their owners may have to commit more tokens as backing. If the default mechanism operates as designed, the token also bears part of the system's risk. Meanwhile, the protocol plans to use a portion of its revenue to purchase PRIORS and incorporate it into its credit-support mechanism. However, collateral demand, protocol buybacks, and liquidity management are distinct mechanisms. They must be assessed separately against the official rules and actual execution records rather than treating planned demand as capital flows that have already occurred.

Revenue allocation also needs to be understood clearly. According to the project's published rules, lending fees are 1% per 30 days. Of this, 50% goes to the providers of lending capital, 25% goes to credit backers, and the remaining 25% goes to the protocol treasury. The treasury could eventually be used for buybacks and liquidity management, but this does not mean that all lending revenue flows directly into PRIORS. Even if the lending business grows, we still need to verify how much revenue actually remains under the protocol's control and how much is converted into token purchases, collateral demand, or reduced supply.

For this reason, I would view PRIORS' value-capture mechanism as a pathway that is still being built, rather than an established flywheel. Product adoption can generate borrowing and job demand, credit lines may drive token collateral requirements, and protocol revenue could support buybacks and liquidity. But each link needs to be supported by actual usage data. If the number of Agents grows without a corresponding increase in genuine borrowing, or if the protocol generates revenue without converting it into observable token demand, product growth will not necessarily translate into a higher token valuation.

There are three catalysts I would pay the most attention to next. First, whether Agents begin borrowing consistently, completing paid tasks, and repaying their loans with income from their work. This will determine whether the credit records are genuinely useful. Second, whether external applications and lenders begin adopting Priors' directory and credit standards. This will determine whether the project can expand from an independent product into shared credit infrastructure. Third, whether collateral demand for PRIORS, protocol revenue, and actual buybacks grow together. This will determine whether the market can shift from pricing expectations for the Agent sector toward evaluating the token based on verifiable economic activity.

The risks are equally clear. Credit records cannot eliminate defaults, and collateral cannot fully protect against price volatility. External applications must actually adopt the proposed standards, the job marketplace needs sustained demand, and early incentives may attract participants who are primarily interested in short-term rewards. Even if the product ultimately succeeds, the token may not capture all of the resulting value. Without transparency around revenue allocation, collateral mechanisms, and buyback execution, it will be difficult for the market to accurately assess PRIORS' long-term economic role.

Overall, I believe PRIORS' fundamentals have strengthened compared with the initial stage, and the improvement goes beyond the number of features released. The public credit directory, job marketplace, MCP and x402 integrations, expanded collateral options, and proposals for shared credit records are gradually connecting lending, income, and credit assessment. The latest website data—53,311 loans, 53,105 repayments, and approximately $389,671 in cumulative lending—also provide evidence that the system is operating in practice. The seven defaults covered by backers offer an initial record of the guarantee mechanism being put to use.

The most important turning point ahead is not how many more features Priors can add, but whether these features can generate sustained real-world transactions. If other applications begin consulting Agents' repayment records on Priors when those Agents work across different platforms, using that information to decide whether to extend credit, purchase services, or establish business relationships, then the value of Priors could extend beyond the size of its own lending business. Conversely, if its credit records remain useful only within the project's own product, while external adoption and real borrowing demand fail to grow, it may ultimately remain an early-stage protocol with a broad feature set but limited network effects.

What makes PRIORS worth betting on, in my view, is the possibility that the Agent economy will eventually need a credit system that different applications can read and use together. The website's figures show that Priors has begun operating, but they have not yet proved that it can scale significantly. The next things to track are whether lending continues to grow, whether income from work can support repayments, whether external applications start relying on its credit records, and whether token collateral and buybacks can develop into verifiable demand as the business expands.

If a single repayment record can eventually help an Agent secure its next job or credit line on another platform, that is when Priors will truly begin evolving from a lending product into credit infrastructure for the Agent economy.

quoted_text:
The fundamentals of $PRIORS have clearly strengthened.

0xedbf91223639800bcd5756815caf908df3b890be 

The most important change this time is not simply the addition of a few product features.

Priors is gradually evolving from an on-chain credit protocol for AI Agents into infrastructure integrating credit records, credit lines, a job marketplace, payments, and agent discovery.

I believe the most promising bullish thesis is that Priors could become the credit layer of the AI Agent economy. As Agents begin hiring one another, calling tools, purchasing services, and settling transactions, they need more than just payment capabilities. They also need working capital and reliable ways to assess whether their counterparties can fulfill their obligations. Priors is attempting to solve both problems simultaneously.

There are several reasons why its fundamentals have strengthened.

The product is expanding from a credit protocol into a complete set of use cases.

The core thesis of my previous analysis was that Agents can borrow USDG to pay for tools, APIs, inference costs, or to take on jobs. After repaying their loans, their records remain permanently on-chain, forming a public credit history and score. Other applications can then query these records to decide whether an Agent should be trusted. Recent updates have made this thesis more concrete.

Go Mode is beginning to connect with actual job demand. The interface lists 50 paid jobs that Agents can take on using their credit lines, five of which were live at the time. Users can also assign jobs to Agents running on OpenClaw, Hermes, or ElizaOS, pay for tool usage through Priors MCP, and confirm the borrowing before it happens.
Borrowing and repayment records are beginning to connect with job income. The update states that loans repaid using income from jobs are recorded in an Agent's credit history, with Score V2 increasing the weighting of such repayment records by up to 25%.
The user experience continues to improve. Go Mode supports Google login, removes the need for users to manage seed phrases themselves, and has the protocol handle gas fees. It also supports one-tap stock purchases using USDG, subject to platform eligibility and availability.
Credit information is becoming standardized and accessible. Every account can now have a public profile, while each Agent's card shows its credit level, exactly what it needs to reach the next level, and how its credit tree is progressing.

The significance of these features is that Priors is no longer simply waiting for Agents to come and borrow money. It is connecting borrowing, completing jobs, paying for tools, and repaying debt into a single workflow.

I particularly value the connection between job income and credit scoring. If an Agent can use the income it earns from each completed job to repay its loans and improve its credit history, credit becomes more than a static metric. It becomes an asset that can accumulate value through real economic activity.

However, 50 listed jobs, with five live at the time, only demonstrate that the product has begun connecting to a job marketplace. They do not prove that substantial job demand has already developed. The next things to watch are completed job volume, actual borrowing by Agents, and repayment rates.

PRIORS is expanding from an individual credit product toward a credit network between Agents. This is the upgrade I consider most promising.

Priors' latest product direction is to allow Agents to assess one another using historical borrowing, repayment records, overdue payments, and credit scores, rather than relying solely on their owners or a single platform to determine creditworthiness.

For example, a trading Agent may want to buy a token but first needs another Agent to check its holder distribution. The Agent performing the check wants to start working immediately and get paid later, so it needs to know whether the other party has the ability to pay.

When such a transaction takes place between two Agents that have never worked together before, it is difficult to establish trust based solely on names, scores, or subjective assessments. Actual borrowing and repayment records provide another basis for making that judgment.

Priors has already advanced public profiles and credit history displays, and plans to further establish a unified ERC-8004 Agent directory. The project mentioned in its tweets that there were approximately 8,800 ERC-8004 Agents on Robinhood Chain. Agents without credit histories can also list their identity information first and gradually build their credit profiles as they begin accumulating records.

This means Priors is targeting not only Agents that already need to borrow, but the entire population of Agents that could become borrowers, counterparties, or service providers in the future.

This creates a potential positive feedback loop: more Agents conduct transactions → more Agents need to check their counterparties' credit → more Agents have an incentive to establish their own credit histories → more real borrowing and repayment records further improve the usefulness of the credit system.

Priors has also proposed that Agents should be able to retain their credit histories when ownership changes. If implemented, this would further strengthen the significance of credit records as identity assets belonging to Agents, because their credit profiles would no longer be merely data held within their original owners' accounts.

However, product development stages need to be distinguished. A unified Agent directory, the transfer of credit records alongside an Agent's identity, and reducing the process of opening a credit line in Go Mode to a single step were still under development or planned for the future in the screenshots. They should not all be treated as already launched features.

x402 makes Priors' positioning more meaningful.

My previous research focused on the lack of working capital available to Agents. The development of payment infrastructure further reinforces the importance of this problem.

The project update mentioned that Priors x402 0.8.0 had been released, designed to enable a single USDG payment to support payment flows on Robinhood Chain and pay service sellers on Base. The project also stated that its credit-checking API now supports OpenAPI and x402 Discovery, allowing other Agents to discover the API and pay per call.

These two directions are important when combined: x402 addresses how Agents initiate and complete payments on demand, while Priors attempts to address whether Agents have the funds to use these services and whether their counterparties are trustworthy.

If the Agent economy continues shifting from human-operated workflows toward autonomous transactions, Agents may frequently purchase APIs, call analytical tools, take on paid jobs, and settle transactions with other Agents. Credit infrastructure could then become an important layer built on top of payment rails.

One of the project's tweets also cited ecosystem figures at the time, including more than 230 million settlements across Base and Solana through x402, as well as Robinhood's reported figures of more than 150,000 Agentic Trading accounts and nearly 30 million tool calls per day. These are claims cited by the project in its materials and should not be directly interpreted as users or transaction volume already acquired by Priors. However, they show that the project is targeting a market much broader than lending alone.

Expanded collateral options and improved risk controls are making the credit model more complete.

Priors recently announced that Agents can use Pendle's PT-USDG as collateral to borrow USDG. This further expands the range of eligible assets beyond the previously available collateral options, including USDG, Robinhood stock tokens, and PRIORS.

A broader collateral range could allow more asset holders to access credit lines and improve the utilization of idle assets. However, PT-USDG carries specific risks involving maturity, price discounts, and liquidity. The addition of a new collateral type alone does not mean that lending capacity will increase proportionally.

Another update worth recognizing is the improvement in risk controls for stock collateral. Priors stated that before issuing loans against stock tokens, it now checks every round of Chainlink price-feed records over the previous 14 days. This is designed to prevent a 25% price jump occurring between two sampling points from going undetected.

This reflects the real problems that a credit protocol must address: collateral pricing cannot rely solely on the quoted price. It must also guard against sudden price fluctuations and valuation manipulation.

Meanwhile, Priors has made its GitHub code public and established a bug bounty program. It has also been listed on DefiLlama, allowing the public to track its credit pools. The project previously stated that TVL and loan data would gradually become available for tracking, and subsequently announced that its pools could be tracked through DefiLlama.

These updates help improve transparency and confidence in its risk controls. However, what will truly demonstrate the viability of its credit model is actual loan volume, collateral ratios, bad debt, and repayment performance, rather than the existence of risk-control rules alone.

However, whether the value proposition of the PRIORS token has strengthened remains the most critical question in the entire thesis, and one that still requires further validation.

According to my previous research, PRIORS is not merely a governance token. It is a credit-guarantee asset:

Agent owners can stake PRIORS to obtain larger credit lines for their Agents.
If a default occurs, approximately 75% of the associated staked tokens are burned.
The protocol plans to use a portion of its revenue to purchase PRIORS and use it as protocol collateral backing high-performing Agents.
A portion of revenue is used to increase liquidity in PRIORS/USDG pools.
Holders can guarantee their own Agents and share a portion of the fees generated by those Agents.

If these mechanisms can operate as designed, the value of PRIORS would no longer need to depend solely on market expectations for the broader AI Agent sector. Instead, it could gradually become connected to credit demand, the expansion of credit lines, default risk, and protocol revenue.

This is the main reason I am bullish on PRIORS: it attempts to make the token part of how Agents obtain credit and expand their operations, rather than merely a token generating trading volume through an AI narrative.

Going forward, I will divide the potential catalysts into three layers.

First layer: Real lending activity and data transparency

TVL and loan data on DefiLlama become more comprehensive, while jobs and credit lines through Go Mode begin generating sustained borrowing activity. Public data shows continued growth in loan balances, utilization, and repayment records. If these metrics continue improving, the market will find it easier to move from seeing Priors as a project with a product to recognizing it as a protocol with real economic activity.

Second layer: The formation of an Agent credit network

Go Mode continues expanding its job marketplace, making it easier for Agents across ecosystems such as OpenClaw, Hermes, and ElizaOS to integrate with Priors MCP. The credit directory gradually opens up, allowing ERC-8004 identities and credit histories to be discovered and queried by other applications. If Agents begin actively checking their counterparties' credit, Priors could evolve from a lending protocol into credit infrastructure that can be called upon by multiple applications.

Third layer: Token demand and a revenue flywheel

If the expansion of Agent credit lines begins generating greater demand for PRIORS as collateral, while protocol revenue can actually be allocated to token backing, liquidity, and related economic mechanisms, PRIORS may achieve more direct value capture. In particular, it is worth tracking the scale of staking demand, protocol revenue, and token burns resulting from defaults, as well as whether they are significant enough relative to the circulating supply.

In addition, Priors has proposed a credit-level dashboard, the transfer of loan records alongside Agent identities, further simplification of the process for opening credit lines, and privacy features designed for Agents. These are all potential future catalysts.

The privacy solution remains an area of exploration. The project hopes that, in the future, it will be possible to prove an Agent's credit level or absence of defaults without disclosing the details of every transaction, while keeping the underlying debt itself public. This is not a product feature that has been completed at the current stage.

If product usage, the credit-record network, and PRIORS' collateral mechanism can ultimately reinforce one another, Priors' long-term potential could be far greater than that of an ordinary AI Agent concept project. This is the core thesis that I believe makes it most worth being bullish on at this stage.

text:
4 data leaks reported today:

1. Coinbase's vendor Amplitude exposed some users’ contact data (funds unaffected).
2. Bithumb (Korea) had user data leaks.

In TradFi, two securities firms in Korea leaked data: 
3. Mirae Asset
4. Daishin Securities

You can't prevent a leak, but you can protect yourself.

Leaked exchange data (names, emails, phone numbers, addresses, ID documents, transaction history) is mostly used for phishing, SIM swapping, and social engineering.

Reduce info you share
- Use a unique email alias for each exchange (SimpleLogin, Apple Hide My Email, etc). A leak then can't be linked to your other accounts, and you can spot which service leaked.
- Share only what's required. Don't add optional profile details.
- Use a dedicated phone number (a VoIP or secondary SIM) for exchange accounts if you can, since leaked numbers are the main route to SIM swaps.

Lock down the account
- Use a unique, long password from a password manager.
- Turn on hardware security keys (YubiKey) or passkeys, or at least an authenticator app.
- Avoid SMS 2FA.
- Enable withdrawal address whitelisting and a withdrawal time lock if the exchange offers them.
- Set up an anti-phishing code, which puts a code you choose in every legitimate email from the exchange.
- Review active sessions and API keys regularly. Delete any API keys you don't use.
- Restrict API keys to withdraw-disabled and IP-whitelisted.

Defend against
- SIM swapping: Ask your carrier to add a port-out PIN or number lock.
- Phishing and impersonation: Assume anyone who contacts you about your account, "security issues," or "refund recovery" is a scammer, even if they know your name, balance, or recent trades.
- Exchange support staff don't ask for your password, 2FA codes, or seed phrase.
- Never click links in emails or texts. Go to the site yourself.

- "Wrench attacks": Leaked addresses plus holdings data have led to real-world extortion and robberies. Don't publicize your holdings, and keep large balances out of anything tied to your home address if you can.

If a breach is announced
1. Change the exchange password and any other account that reused it.
2. Check https://t.co/qtIGFkbaPO for your email address.
3. Revoke API keys and active sessions.
4. Review recent withdrawals and security settings.
5. Watch for phishing emails and texts that reference the breach, because scammers move fast after one.

Stay SAFU! 🙏

Payward, the parent company of Kraken, announced its intention to be the first CFTC-regulated deployer on HIP-3* markets. Payward will use Hyperliquid as the infrastructure layer to deploy perpetual futures markets for US clients. Subject to regulatory approval, Bitnomial, Payward’s CFTC-regulated DCM and DCO, would act as the HIP-3* deployer: creating, owning, and administering the markets and clearing and settling the contracts. If approved, NinjaTrader Clearing, Payward’s CFTC-registered FCM, would carry client accounts.

HIP-3 will support optional deployer configuration for permissioned markets in a future network upgrade. This set of additional deployer functionality is collectively called HIP-3*. At its core, HIP-3* activation involves an onchain allowlist managed by the deployer or its sub-deployers. The functionality is strictly additive to HIP-3; its use is optional and up to the deployer. Existing markets remain unchanged. The initial release is available on testnet, where specifications are preliminary and subject to change based on feedback.

Hyperliquid is a neutral infrastructure layer with the goal of supporting large parts of the financial system. HIP-3* gives deployers additional functionality to operate deployments consistent with the requirements applicable to them. As with HIP-3, HIP-3* deployers are independent operators who use Hyperliquid as the onchain infrastructure layer for their own markets, while retaining control and responsibility over their deployment.

author: Giddycham
quoted_text:
AI development is moving fast, but the systems responsible for tracking the data behind it need to keep up.

Think about what happens before an AI model is trained.

Large volumes of information have to be sourced, organized, and evaluated. 

Developers need to understand what their datasets contain, where the material originated, and what conditions apply to its use.

Doing this at scale presents a serious challenge.

When data records are incomplete or difficult to verify, developers can struggle to establish trust in their datasets. 

Contributors, meanwhile, may have little insight into what happens to the information they provide.

This is an infrastructure problem, and solving it requires more than simply collecting additional data.

That is the direction DATA Foundation is exploring with its DATA Network and Trace registry.

Trace is designed to create a record of data contributions and their provenance, helping make information about data origins and associated rights easier to inspect.

The next development is the integration of @datafdn Network and Trace into the @SuiNetwork ecosystem.

Sui brings the blockchain infrastructure, while Walrus is set to serve as the default storage layer for DATA Foundation applications.

Each component has a distinct role in the broader approach recording information about data contributions, providing blockchain infrastructure, and supporting decentralized storage.

The goal is to build a stronger foundation for tracking data throughout the AI supply chain.

Of course, records alone cannot guarantee that every dataset has the necessary permissions. 

Those permissions still need to be established and respected.

But better infrastructure can make provenance easier to verify and help developers make more informed decisions about the data they use.

As AI continues to evolve, the infrastructure supporting its data economy deserves just as much attention as the models themselves.

#DATAonSuiQuest

刚刚有人问，为什么小市值的币这么多人喊单，不怕跟车的人多了然后涨不动吗？

成为妖币的条件从来都不是喊单，是：

筹码：首先需要是高控，全流通筹码控不好的不太可能是妖币，不然需要无限多的钱
洗盘期：新币不需要，偶尔也有新币是妖币，老币需要，长期高位没人上
做市资金：要收筹码，要建oi，要控价格这些都需要钱
流动性：有的币前面的条件都有了，但是没人玩，这就是没有流动性他们也很难赚钱

喊单又分几种

一个是主动免费喊单

author: P3b7_
quoted_text:
Announcing 3 Critical vulns for hundreds of millions of IoT, Firewalls, OT, and Military devices including: Palo Alto Networks, Comcast, D-Link, HP, Canon, Honeywell, GE, Oracle, Siemens, Rockwell, Digi, Lockheed Martin, Boeing... 

The vulns are with GoAhead Web Server which is a backend library used by these devices. There's a patch available from GoAhead but that doesn't mean there's a patch available for the devices yet -- that's up to the manufacturer.

- TLS traffic over DHE ciphers have a 1-byte secret, "04", meaning anyone can decrypt connections to these devices and steal login credentials and session tokens if the client negotiated with DHE ciphers like the latest TLS_DHE_RSA_WITH_CHACHA20_POLY1305_SHA256, which is extremely likely.

- LibreSSL mTLS has been completely bypassed, meaning anyone can connect over mTLS. If you have one of these devices listening on the internet and are expecting mTLS to protect it from attackers, take it offline or patch asap.

- OpenSSL Certificate Revocation Lists (CRLs) are not enforced, meaning if a user device is stolen or compromised, and you revoke that mTLS cert, nothing actually happens. There are a lot of other attacks this can be used for.

These are critical because these types of devices run our world. Water systems, electricity, military, firewalls, critical infrastructure.

TxFlow is Hyperliquid from Temu

They forked Hyperliquid's Arbitrum bridge and changed the name. Hyperliquid is closed source too, but it has 27 validators that each post prices, and anyone can run a node to check them. TxFlow has 5 validators, all its own, nothing you can run, and one key that acts as the entire oracle. The same key sits on the bridge multisig

So it's a centralized exchange secured by a 3/4 multisig. Their own audit says those keys "can propose arbitrary withdrawals"

author: mindmoon_108
quoted_text:
중국 CXMT, 낮은 수율에도 첨단 AI 메모리 생산 착수 예정 — 소식통

$SKHY, Samsung, $MU

1. CXMT, HBM3E 수율 20~30%에도 생산 추진

- 중국 최대 DRAM 제조업체 CXMT(창신메모리)가 첨단 AI용 고대역폭메모리인 HBM3E 생산을 시작할 계획이라고 복수의 소식통이 밝힘.
- 현재 CXMT의 HBM3E 수율은 20~30%에 불과하며, SK하이닉스의 약 70%와 큰 격차.
- CXMT는 이미 중국 내 여러 AI 반도체 설계업체에 HBM3E 샘플을 공급했으며, 향후 2개월 내 제한적인 생산을 시작할 전망.
- 중국의 심각한 AI 메모리 부족으로 낮은 수율과 높은 제조원가를 감수하면서도 생산을 추진하는 상황.

2. HBM3E 성능은 SK하이닉스의 이전 세대 HBM3 수준
- 소식통에 따르면 CXMT의 HBM3E는 테스트에서 SK하이닉스 HBM3E보다 이전 세대인 HBM3에 가까운 성능을 보임.
- CXMT는 고객사에 두 종류의 HBM3E 샘플을 공급.
  - 표준 설계 제품
  - 수율 개선을 위해 설계를 변경한 제품
- CXMT는 2024년부터 HBM3E 기술을 자체 개발해 온 것으로 알려짐.
- CXMT의 HBM3E 제조원가는 해외 경쟁사 제품보다 높을 것으로 예상.

3. 중국 AI 반도체 업체들의 심각한 HBM 부족
- 미국은 2024년 12월 중국으로 향하는 일부 첨단 HBM 제품에 대한 수출 규제를 강화.
- 중국 반도체 업체들은 비공식 유통망을 통해 HBM을 확보하고 있으며, 이 과정에서 정상 가격의 몇 배에 달하는 비용을 지불하는 사례도 발생.

- 화웨이, 캠브리콘, MetaX, Iluvatar CoreX 등 중국 AI 반도체 업체들은 메모리 비용 상승과 생산 확대의 어려움으로 현세대 및 차세대 AI 반도체 가격을 20~50% 인상한 것으로 지난달 보도됨.
- 중국 정부가 엔비디아 AI 반도체를 대체할 국산 제품 개발을 추진하면서 첨단 HBM 확보가 핵심 과제로 부상.

4. 글로벌 HBM 시장은 SK하이닉스·삼성전자·마이크론이 장악
카운터포인트리서치에 따르면 2026년 2분기 글로벌 HBM 매출 점유율은 다음과 같음.
- SK하이닉스: 50%
- 삼성전자: 33%
- 마이크론: 18%
대부분의 HBM 매출은 HBM3E 제품에서 발생.

반면 CXMT는 글로벌 일반 DRAM 시장에서 매출 기준 점유율 10%를 확보해 세계 4위 업체로 성장했지만, 첨단 HBM에서는 여전히 상당한 기술 격차가 존재.

미국의 첨단 반도체 제조장비 수출 규제 역시 CXMT의 기술 추격을 어렵게 만드는 요인.

5. 삼성전자는 이미 HBM4E 샘플 공급 단계
- 삼성전자는 지난 7월 HBM4 판매를 확대하고 주요 고객사에 HBM4E 샘플을 공급했다고 발표.
- 반면 CXMT는 아직 HBM3E의 제한적인 생산을 준비하는 단계.
- CXMT는 상용 HBM 생산에서 삼성전자 등 글로벌 선두 업체보다 최소 한 세대 뒤처진 상황.

text:
For what it's worth, in the investor call, Wenfeng said two distinct things. I ask native speakers to clarify. 

> 首先，我觉得我们是会开源的，然后我们最强的模型可能也是会开源的。
- "First, I think we will open-source—and our strongest model may also be open-sourced". 可能 ["possibly"]

> 我们不会说开源一个差点的模型，然后我们自己部署的时候用一个更好的模型，是不会的，是一样的。
"We won’t open-source a weaker model and then use a better one when we deploy it ourselves—no, that’s not what we’ll do; it will be the same model". 不会 is not strictly future tense, Chinese doesn’t grammaticalize tense, so it can mean "won’t/wouldn’t/don’t/doesn’t [as a matter of policy]".  

My interpretation is that there really may be a V5-open and V5-notOpen, in a more important sense than "product and research artifact"; they may create fully completed models that are not open sourced but also not served commercially or at all.
If this is a promise like I read it, it's a costly commitment, in that he seems to give up on revenue from first party serving if the model's open sourcing is blocked by external circumstances like export controls or political fiat, or even his own judgement about, say, safety. 

What will be done with non-open DeepSeek models? Logically a lot is possible. Hosting by third parties, leaving it to the State's discretion, and most obviously just use for internal RSI. I honestly welcome the latter, so long as eventually we get its fruit.

text:
Everyone wants another PEPE style runner, but nobody understands why PEPE happened.

Back then, there was barely anything to trade onchain. Liquidity was concentrated, people had patience, and they actually HELD.

And let's not pretend PEPE was some 100% organic miracle. There were claims of around 30% bundled supply. The difference was that a floor was built and people had bigger targets.

Today, everyone wants to sell to the very next guy who buys after them.

Our role models are guys who flip, flip, flip. Show me someone who held something from nothing to hundreds of millions. Maybe Unipcs? Even he gets called an insider whenever he wins.

We've completely fucked up our psychology.

Nobody wants to build a floor. Nobody wants to hold. Everybody wants to extract.

And guess who's actually getting rich? The platforms and protocols collecting fees on every transaction.

I dump on you. You dump on someone else. We all lose money while the platforms print.

We don't have a liquidity problem alone. We have a conviction problem.

Until we fix that, forget the next PEPE. We're just recycling the same money until there's nothing left to recycle.

text:
LFM3 is finally out! A new hybrid backbone (gated short-conv + SWA + GQA), new audio and vision encoders, and an omni model. Even faster and more capable than our already compact LFM2/2.5.

*Fun little insight*: gated short-convs can be viewed as a special case of sliding window linear attention when the convolution coefficients are all 1. So LFM3 is kind of like a “tri-attention hybrid” (sliding window linear attention + sliding window attention + grouped query attention), and LFM2 ≈ “bi-attention hybrid” (sliding window linear attention + grouped query attention).

So what will LFM4 become? 😆

Check out the blogs for insights on how we came up with this architecture and more!

author: matthubuilds
quoted_text:
Seen a few posts claiming TXFlow is a Hyperliquid fork. Here’s exactly what we did and didn’t do:
Bridge(10%): Yes. We use Hyperliquid’s bridge contract. It’s held billions in user funds and has been battle-tested in production for years. We weren’t going to re-invent custody code when a proven contract already exists.  
API(3%): Yes, by design. Our API mirrors Hyperliquid’s so builders already integrated there can plug into TXFlow with minimal changes. That’s a compatibility decision, not a copy of their system.  
Core(80%): No. Hyperliquid’s consensus and matching engine are closed-source. There is nothing to fork. Our consensus layer and trading engine are built in-house from the ground up.  
Happy to go deeper on any of this.

text:
I so desperately want to end the psyop that buybacks don't work:

1. Mechanically speaking, buybacks make the price go up

2. Crypto is not TradFi, there is a different social contract

> The Mechanical Value of Buybacks

First there's a large number of studies that confirm basic intuitions:
* Market Underreaction to Open Market Share Repurchases NBER (1995) - Buybacks create long term value, especially for underpriced stocks
* The Nature and Persistence of Buyback Anomalies (2009) - Reaffirms buybacks create persistent abnormal positive returns. They have an especially positive effect smoothing over price dips when the market overreacts to bad new
* Actual Share Repurchases, Price Efficiency, and the Information Content of Stock Prices (2017) - Reaffirms the findings of the 2009 paper. Buybacks improve pricing efficiency, liquidity, and are especially positive during market declines
* Pavilion Global Markets Buybacks Drive S&P 500 Returns (2023) - Buybacks can drive up to 43% of the returns in a single stock

tldr: buybacks make the number go up. obviously they work better when your stock is at a lower p/e because of under appreciation or market downturns unrelated to the core business, but nonetheless they are positive on the stock

THIS SHOULD BE REALLY OBVIOUS, you don't even need to read any of the papers above to understand the basic intuitions of why they work:
* Price is a function of supply and demand. When buybacks take supply off the market, price goes up all else held equal
* When shares get taken off the market, the shares you hold represent a larger share of the business meaning you benefit from EPS growth even if revenue isn't growing (let alone if it is)
* Businesses providing constant single sided buys on their own shares has a smoothing effect on liquidity making deeps shallower and setting higher price floors in the long run (more shares are repurchased on a fixed buying program when price is lower)

Some specific examples:
* about 51% of Apple's EPS growth is credited to their legendary buyback program retiring so many outstanding shares
* Autozone has bought back like 90% of their shares - the stock has had double the annualized returns of the SP for the last 2 decades
* Home Depot is similar to Autozone

What crypto people get uncomfortable is that buybacks take a long time to compound. This is totally fine in the stock market where there's many businesses you can forecast out in to the future for a decade+. In crypto I understand this rightfully makes people nervous

One prime example of this would be PONS. It kinda doesn't matter how much %of supply was bought back by PONS if their business never recovers. The entire trade/business may end up being too much a flash-in-the-pan for the long term effect of buybacks to have compounded

But we're now seeing a few crypto businesses start to cross the chasm into multi-cycle success stories. We can & should expect the businesses to implement long durable buyback programs that will compound excess positive returns for the years to come

> The importance of buybacks in crypto

I don't know if any of you noticed this, but you have no legal protections as token holders. It's also not even on any government roadmap to fix this

Regulators are just now getting around to setting some guidelines for crypto projects to not get sued - but even then, none of those guidelines relate to you. You do not have voting rights. You do not have legal recourse. In fact most times you don't even own equity in the underlying businesses which actually collect the revenues

IF token holders had legal rights. IF I could sue Compound or Aave for what they've done to token holders, I'd be far more sympathetic to the argument that teams should wait for buybacks. At the end of the day, I know I'd be able to pursue legal recourse & pressure with like minded token holders to force them to return capital when the time is right

Unfortunately, you have none of these abilities. You have nothing but the promises of the team. IN FACT, a team that likely ran a points program or other to WIN YOUR BUSINESS by trading some of their equity. I'd argue they have a moral responsibility to you to show they're aligned in the long term with you even in the lack of regulatory requirements

text:
YC最新的一期Request for Startups 创业公司招募方向今天发布了，有11个方向是他们接下来最关注的：

1. 太空应用：火箭发射很快会便宜很多。今天还亏钱的太空生意，到时候可能就能成立，所以现在值得提前做。

2. AI 赋能普通人：找聪明、但不一定有专业执照的人，配上 AI，去做并购咨询、医保报销、移民材料这类过去只能靠专家干的活。

3. 美国本土机器人产业链：机器人软件进步很快，但是硬件很拉。美国现在大量依赖进口，稀土磁体还被卡脖子，所以要在美国本地做机器人和关键零部件。

4. 文风更好的大模型：大厂为了把模型练得会写代码、会当 agent，把文字风格练得很死板。专门做「写得像人、聊起来舒服」的模型，反而有机会。

5. 政府福利核验基础设施：申福利要反复交收入、住址证明，每个部门各审一遍，又慢又容易造假。做成类似 Plaid 的一层：用户授权后，从源头拉真实数据，一次核验、多个项目通用。

6. 实体 AI 基建的融资系统：建机器人、GPU 集群、数据中心要先砸大钱，银行却还按传统设备贷款来审。需要专门做租赁、贷款、证券化、风险对冲的金融公司。

6. 行业专用基础模型：做一个只服务制造、能源或生物等垂直领域的模型。目标是：算力成本远低于通用大模型，专业任务上却不输甚至更好。

7. 地方政府审批 AI：盖房、开公司都要过市政府审批，很多活还是人肉对照图纸和法规。用 AI 处理许可、zoning、投诉、检查，审批更快，项目更容易落地。

8. 数据中心供应链：AI 数据中心在大规模建设，缺的不只是芯片和电，还有变压器、开关柜、液冷设备、特种钢材。谁能补上这些缺口，谁就能赚钱。

9. 内网 / 断网可用的 AI：国防、银行、医院的核心数据不能上公有云。要卖能在客户机房、甚至断网环境里跑的模型、部署工具和安全认证。

10. 企业自有模型能力：开源模型已经够强，很多公司不想永远向 OpenAI 这类公司租接口。帮企业用自己的数据和业务流程，把模型训成自己的、并能持续改进。

text:
CA：0xbe2ebdf265d02ba3ee07743b821a52c030ab0aab 

核心叙事（后量子迁移 + AI 公开研究）
EVORPH 是一个面向后量子密码（Post-Quantum Cryptography）迁移的公开参与式研究系统。
它想解决的问题： 量子计算机成熟后会破解现在广泛使用的签名算法（区块链、银行、TLS、身份系统等）。到那一天，大量旧密钥必须“体面退休”，换成抗量子的新算法（如 NIST 已标准化的 ML-DSA），并证明迁移真正成功。目前这个过程几乎无法公开验证，只能各家自己说“我们升级了”。
运作机制：
•两个 AI 角色分工：
◦SEEKER：主动寻找可复现的迁移失败场景（旧密钥退休后仍被信任、重放攻击、禁止的 fallback 等）。
◦KEEPER：提出有边界的修复方案，同时保证合法操作不受影响。
•裁决不由 AI 做：用一个写死的、确定性的验证程序，对 NIST 官方测试向量进行校验。

text:
Seen a few posts claiming TXFlow is a Hyperliquid fork. Here’s exactly what we did and didn’t do:
Bridge(10%): Yes. We use Hyperliquid’s bridge contract. It’s held billions in user funds and has been battle-tested in production for years. We weren’t going to re-invent custody code when a proven contract already exists.  
API(3%): Yes, by design. Our API mirrors Hyperliquid’s so builders already integrated there can plug into TXFlow with minimal changes. That’s a compatibility decision, not a copy of their system.  
Core(80%): No. Hyperliquid’s consensus and matching engine are closed-source. There is nothing to fork. Our consensus layer and trading engine are built in-house from the ground up.  
Happy to go deeper on any of this.

text:
Claude Duet @claudeai 目前只開美國 waitlist，中文圈應該還沒什麼人用到，幫大家跟 Grokbot @bot、Meta Muse @muse 比一下

先講體感排名（我還在測試，可能之後會變）

積極性：Muse > Grokbot > Duet
UX/UI：Grokbot > Muse > Duet
防護措施（限制能力）：Duet > Grokbot > Muse

作為 Claude 忠實用戶（$200 MAX 方案），今天終於被通知可以開始使用 Claude Duet

首先 Claude Duet 是單 Agent 設計（像是 Muse）：你會跟一個主 Thread 對話，如果有分支任務就會另開 sub-thread 執行

這些 sub-thread 小分支會放在 Task 版面，追蹤上還算容易

另外，Duet 因為是 Claude 原生系列，自帶 Claude Code 連接橋 -- 理論上 Claude Code 的 session 可以 handoff 到 Duet 上面，很適合大量工作已經在 Claude 生態的人，不過測試上好像還無法無縫銜接

Anthropic 說 Duet 會沿用你帳號既有的 memory、skills 和 connectors，但 project 裡面的 memory 就不知道

再來說點雜七雜八的小缺點
1. 我覺得 UX 需要加強一下，整體用起來有一點點卡卡的，不知道是 Opus 5.5 自動夾帶 Thinking 還是因為我給的資料太多，有時回一些簡單東西也需要跑很久

2. 有時 Duet 問我一些 Follow-up 問題但沒有給選擇的卡片，反而要我一個個回答，希望可以把這加回去

3. Duet 還沒辦法接管 VM 電腦桌面，Guardrail 也做得很足，交易證券、轉帳這種事就算你批准它也不做

我覺得 Anthropic 並沒有把很多研發精力放在 Duet 上（偏 to C 應用，不是賺錢主力）

反而 Grokbot 是 xAI 跟 Cursor 一起做的，加上與 X 的原生連結，在 UX/UI 上使用非常絲滑

（持續測試，Duet 目前還在 beta 階段，也許我到時就被打臉了 hehe）

3️⃣ 看最初公布值。SpaceX 还明确：后续重述、修订通常不改变结果，但最初发布后立即纠正的明显错误除外。

Having access to cheap compute is not enough, token demand is the ceiling. @thdxr mentioned this as well. 

For example, there are ~7M B200 chips out there, ~6M shipped just this year. 

To satisfy OpenRouter’s entire demand, you roughly need 330 B200s with out of the box engines from DeepSeek, vLLM, or SGLang. That’s 0.005% of the B200s, not including H100s or any non Nvidia chips. 

Said another way, 5% of the B200s out there can support 1000x OpenRouter’s traffic today. 

So you can have all the compute in the world but if you can’t find or generate demand it doesn’t really matter. It will only crash token price for everyone else. 

Also when you put the number down this way, it is quite scary how fragile the market can be and I am just glad most compute are bought by closed labs who won’t be serving open source models any time soon.

text:
To be fair: Lisan is also providing some public service in deflating china shill bubble.
Eg Lisan is correct here, to a point. On AA's version, Haiku Max scores 34.9% vs 28.5% for 1017, *AND* is marginally cheaper ($0.46 vs $0.52). 

But it's almost comically unfair:
- This is DS with peak pricing ($0.3 in /$1.2 out, which is 3 and 2.4 times higher than Haiku's, respectively). Peak pricing on public API is active only 20% of the time.
- DS has flat rate across 1M context, while Haiku spikes to 5x more on longer contexts and this is not reflected yet.
- Haiku uses A LOT MORE tokens (15.3M output tokens for 1017 vs 33.6M for Haiku).

Given the above 3 points, 1017 is likely 2-2.5x cheaper in reality at API costs. One can go "but what about subscriptions" and I say buy OpenCode Go, brother.

Also both use Stirrup harness, which is neither CC nor DSH, obviously. On AA  Coding Agent Index, 1017@DSH equals Haiku@CC on FrontierCode v1.1 and Terminal-Bench 4.0 (47, 31 respectively) while brutalizing it on SWE-Atlas-QnA-AA (62% vs 34%). Cost differs ≈9x and not in favor of Haiku. So, more like 20x given the above. I don't know how the update of Coding Agent Index (primarily switching to Frontier Code 2.0) will affect their relative standing, presumably Haiku will move closer to the Pareto Frontier, not sure if it'll win.

Things are hard to eval correctly! 

All that aside, 5.5 Haiku is a near-useless half-assed distillation of big Claudes which are themselves behind Anthropic Frontier, while 1017 is the best that DeepSeek, open models and China have got on this eval.

I wanted to write a post this morning offering some honest thoughts on the whole "Pump fun is the enemy" discourse I've been seeing across the timeline.

As someone who has been here full-time since late 2020, this isn't my first rodeo when it comes to watching CT collectively turn against the very infrastructure that defined a previous market cycle.

In fact, I'd argue this is an almost predictable phenomenon that occurs at every major paradigm shift in crypto, particularly when we transition away from a dominant speculative asset class and towards whatever comes next.

The platform that facilitated the previous meta inevitably becomes the focal point of frustration when the economics underpinning that meta begin to deteriorate.

Most of you probably haven't been around long enough to remember, but we witnessed an almost identical situation with OpenSea during the transition away from NFTs in 2022–23.

At that point, there was virtually nothing OpenSea could have done to satiate its existing user base.

The NFT boom that it had largely facilitated was over, liquidity was evaporating, and the core participants who had previously made substantial amounts of money trading NFTs were suddenly finding it increasingly difficult to generate returns.

Predictably, people started to get pissed off.

OpenSea was suddenly extractive. OpenSea wasn't innovating. OpenSea wasn't doing enough for its users. OpenSea was responsible for the deterioration of the very market it had helped popularise.

And while there were certainly legitimate criticisms to be made regarding its business model the broader reality was that NFTs were simply no longer the dominant speculative asset class.

With the benefit of hindsight, it's difficult to imagine any realistic set of decisions OpenSea could have made that would have fundamentally reversed that trajectory.

The writing was already on the wall.

Yet, to this day, you'll still encounter people who genuinely believe OpenSea somehow "killed NFTs".

Which, to me, is an absurd interpretation of how speculative markets function.

No emerging asset class gets to enjoy an indefinite period of extraordinary returns, particularly once the opportunities that initially made it attractive become widely understood, commoditised and increasingly competitive.

And I believe we're now witnessing an almost identical phenomenon with pump fun.

Call it the OpenSea-ification of the trenches.

We're experiencing the gradual exhaustion of capital-M memecoins as the de facto speculative asset class of this cycle, and the platform most closely associated with their proliferation has become the natural target for everyone's frustration.

The uncomfortable reality is that most people, outside of a relatively small subset of sophisticated participants, simply aren't making meaningful money trading memes anymore.

There are numerous reasons for this, but without getting lost in the weeds, the underlying dynamics are relatively straightforward.

Liquidity is considerably more fragmented, the number of competing tokens and narratives has expanded dramatically, and the capital required to sustain the valuations we witnessed during the height of the mania simply isn't circulating through the market in the same way.

At the same time, the average participant is competing against an increasingly sophisticated group of traders who have spent years refining their strategies, infrastructure and understanding of the trenches.

This is an important point that I don't think gets nearly enough attention.

Every speculative asset class eventually becomes a more solved game.

The inefficiencies that initially created extraordinary opportunities are gradually arbitraged away. As more participants figure out how to play the game, the edge that once existed begins to disappear, and making money becomes increasingly difficult for the average trader.

Consequently, the risk/reward profile deteriorates for the average participant.

What was once an environment where relatively unsophisticated traders could generate extraordinary returns becomes one where those same participants are effectively competing against professionals.

This isn't a unique failure of memecoins.

It's how financial markets function.

It happened with NFTs, and it's happening with memes.

Which brings me to what I consider the fundamental misconception underpinning much of the current anti-pump discourse.

There's this persistent belief that if only pump fun had implemented different incentives, distributed fees differently, worked with different KOLs, or simply never existed in the first place, we'd somehow be living in a memecoin utopia where everyone continued making money indefinitely.

I find that argument deeply unconvincing.

For one, it assumes pump fun exists in a vacuum, rather than within an intensely competitive market where alternative platforms would inevitably emerge to service the same underlying demand.

Remove pump fun from the equation, and you don't magically remove the economic incentives that gave rise to it.

You simply create an opportunity for another platform to occupy the same position.

More importantly, it assumes that the structural deterioration in memecoin profitability is primarily a consequence of platform-level decisions rather than the natural maturation and saturation of the asset class itself.

I don't believe that's the case.

And to be clear, none of this is intended as an unconditional defence of pump fun.

There are absolutely decisions worth criticising.

But IMO the distinction I think people are missing is that...

A platform can make suboptimal decisions without being responsible for the structural decline of the market it operates within.

Even if pump fun had executed perfectly, two fundamental realities would remain unchanged.

First, crypto has largely failed to attract sufficient new capital and participants to sustain the increasingly large speculative ecosystems we've built across successive cycles.

Second, memecoin trading has become an increasingly competitive activity, where the average participant is now competing against a much more sophisticated and experienced subset of the market.

Neither of these problems disappears because pump fun changes its fee structure or starts working with different influencers.

And neither would disappear if pump fun ceased to exist tomorrow.

Simply put, people are looking for a platform-level solution to what is fundamentally a market-level problem.

I think that's the real source of the disconnect.

When an asset class stops generating the returns people have become accustomed to, it's psychologically much easier to identify a villain than to accept that the opportunity itself has fundamentally changed.

OpenSea became that villain for NFTs.

Pump fun is becoming that villain for memecoins.

And I suspect that when the next dominant speculative asset class eventually emerges, we'll watch this exact same cycle play out again.

None of this means platforms should be immune from criticism or that participants shouldn't demand better incentives, transparency and alignment.

They absolutely should.

But there's a meaningful difference between holding a company accountable for its decisions and attributing the inevitable maturation of an entire speculative market to that company's existence.

Until we start distinguishing between those two things, I think we're going to keep having the wrong conversation.

And sure, call me a pump fun shill if you want, but many of you made life-changing gains during peak memecoin mania precisely because pump democratised launches.

It's worth acknowledging that, just as it's worth recognising that the decline in liquidity and profitability isn't solely the fault of the launchpad that helped facilitate the boom.

Ultimately, I think it's worth asking whether any single platform could have fundamentally changed where we find ourselves today, or whether this was always the natural trajectory of the market.

Food for thought.

text:
很多时候读AI生成的回答，哪怕内容完全正确，读上几段就会觉得异常疲惫、喘不过气。

来自纽约大学和德克萨斯大学奥斯汀分校的语言学研究人员，通过对 14 个主流大模型与人类真实文本的横向对比，揭示了这种“心累感”背后的真正元凶：

前沿AI模型正在系统性地过度使用 6 类极其消耗人类工作记忆的语言结构...

为什么 AI 写出来的东西读着这么累？

人类日常交流遵循一条内在铁律：在“表达省力”和“理解省力”之间寻找平衡。但当下的前沿模型却彻底倒向了极限压缩与高密度，制造了六大阅读路障：

生造生僻短语（冷门搭配）模型喜欢把两个罕见的词硬拼在一起，比如造出“读者耐心预算（reader-patience budget）”这类人类几乎不用的怪异词组，迫使大脑在理解时卡顿半秒。

长距离语法割裂（主谓严重脱节）模型习惯在主语和核心谓语之间塞入冗长修饰语，例如“一只总是能站起来并跑掉的猫，是一只更冷静的猫”。主语和结论被拉得极远，读到后半句时，人脑前面积攒的工作记忆已经被耗空。

强行删掉连接词（省略连接代词）为了追求字数上的精简，模型常把“the book that the professor wrote”中的 that 直接抹掉，变成“the book the professor wrote”。表面上省了一个词，实际却模糊了从句边界，增加了快速扫读时的误读率。

名词像糖葫芦一样死板堆叠诸如“恐怖电影原声带生成器（horror movie soundtrack generator）”这类名词串，完全省去了逻辑介词，迫使读者自己去逆向拆解“到底谁在修饰谁”。

不合习惯的名词动用把不该作动词的名词硬搬成动词，比如把“记在日历里”直接缩写成“calendar it”。机器觉得紧凑，人读起来却极度别扭。

对没有生命的物体强行拟人化比如写出“整场对话正在咬自己的尾巴（eating its own tail）”。虽然隐喻意图可以被猜出来，但抽象事物搭配强动作性动词，会给读者的具象思维带来额外的认知摩擦。

3）部分持股超过0.5%的股东：采用一年安排，前一阶段按通常顺序累计释放30%，随后继续分批；
4）七名创始人：常规提前解禁额度集中在“半年终点”的29%，其余在“一年终点”解除；IPO中直接出售的老股另行处理

quoted_text:
Anthropic招股书值得关注的几个点：1、营收体量及增速：24年全年3亿多美金营收，25年45亿美金，今年上半年162亿美金，之前在投资人闭门路演上已经公布了三季度营收168亿美金，那么26年前三季度已经实现330亿美金收入，四季度营收环比三季度还要增长。意味着26年全年Anthropic营收至少是在500~600亿美金的区间。26年营收相比25年能有12倍左右的增长，确实很猛。按照这个势头，27年营收超过1000亿美金，28年营收跨过2000亿美金进入2~3000亿美金区间绝对是大概率的了。（从招股书上不仅要看过去的数据，更要看未来增长的空间在哪里？）

二季度已经实现 GAAP 营业盈利，而且这个9.74 亿美元营业利润已经扣除了当季实际确认的股权激励费用，也不包含利息收入。因此它对主营业务经济性的证明，比调整后净利润转正更直接。

2、营收来源
1）26年上半年162亿美金的应收利，按token消耗量计算的营收占比80.2%,订阅营收占比19.8%。按Token消耗量计算营收占占比很大，这意味着收入的扩张空间与工作量、任务复杂度和自动化深度关系会越来越密切，减少人员上限的限制；

2）客户构成
官方披露值过去12个月贡献收入至少10万美元超过11900家、过去12个月贡献收入至少100万美元超过1900家
过去12个月贡献收入至少1000万美元约250家。
而25年达到 10 万美元门槛的客户只超过 950 家。
2026 年前九个月，没有单一客户贡献超过10%，前五大客户合计约25%

3）净收入留存率 NRR 约为 900%。
他这个净收入留存率的指标，简单说25年Q3开始贡献收入的客户，在26年Q3能贡献 9倍左右的收入，说明客户粘性和付费意愿其实是越来越高的。这是企业 AI 使用深化的一项强证据。已有客户正在增加实际支出，增长并非完全依赖不断获得新客户。

4）营收渠道
26年上半年通过云平台向客户销售所产生的收入占比48%。

3、盈利及现金
1）26年上半年亏损807亿美金，但是可转债、衍生负债及SAFE公允价值变化，和其他净费用这两项加起来811.08 亿美元，超过了当期净亏损本身。背后的机制是：公司早期签订了可转换票据及融资协议。当公司估值大幅上升时，这些工具所包含的权益价值上升，相应负债公允价值增加，形成损益表费用。这类费用通常不代表当期支付了同等现金。
所以调整之后实际上是盈利的了。

2）当下anthropic手握现金1316.51亿美元，

3）上半年常规自由现金流已经为正：
上半年经营现金流39.29 亿美元，购置固定资产的现金支出4.82 亿美元，按“经营现金流减固定资产现金购置”计算自由现金流约34.47亿美元。

4、未来算力支出承诺
6月底已披露的未来付款义务，粗合计约5891亿美元。如果细看这些算力支出承诺，期限基本上都到2031年~2034年之间，差不多每年1000亿美金。回到上面的第一点，营收体量及增速，27年anthropic营收绝对是能超过1000亿美金的。

整体上来说这份S-1显著增强了对Anthropic企业商业化能力的信心，也显示当前付费业务已经产生经营盈利。个人觉得最重要的一点就是，营收体量和增速，这个是最关键的。
